The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems

Artur Sepp ††thanks: LGT Bank, Zurich, Switzerland (artursepp@gmail.com).    Vladimir Lucic ††thanks: Marex Solutions, London, and Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom (v.lucic@imperial.ac.uk).
This version: July 20, 2026
Abstract

We present a unified approach to designing trend-following (TF) systems and classify them into European, American, and Time Series Momentum categories. For European TF systems, we derive an exact relationship between profit-and-loss, autocorrelation, and drift in volatility-normalized returns. We analyze the expected return under fractional ARFIMA processes and show that TF systems are profitable when the long-term autocorrelation is positive, even under short-term mean reversion. In the frequency domain, the expected return is represented as a Poisson-kernel reading of the analytical or empirical spectrum of the volatility-normalized returns: the system profits at zero drift when the kernel-weighted spectral mass exceeds one, so trend-following alpha is excess spectral mass at low frequencies. Longer lookbacks benefit in addition from the squared drift of the return process. We derive the closed-form Sharpe ratio, with the excess kurtosis of the innovations entering through a single loading, and the net Sharpe ratio and cost-optimal span under trading costs. Under white noise, we derive the closed-form skewness of aggregated TF returns, which is positive at every horizon and peaks near half the filter span. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the analytical results. We show that the positive skewness of TF returns is structural under various model assumptions. Empirically, we evaluate the systems on liquid contracts, and show that all TF systems are strongly correlated and our analytical results can be applied for their performance attribution. Our results enable design, simulation, and performance attribution of TF systems from trend persistence, mean reversion, drift, and skewness.

Key words. Trend-Following Strategies, Managed Futures, Fractional Processes, Autocorrelation, Sharpe Ratio, JEL classification: G11, C22, C58, G17

AMS subject classifications. 91G10, 62M10, 60G10

1 Introduction

Trend-following systems have been employed by many quantitative and discretionary funds, also known as commodity trading advisors (CTAs), or managed futures, since the early 1980s. The industry traces back to the turtle-trading classes of Richard Dennis in the early 1980s (Angrist, 1989), whose graduates created quantitatively driven CTA funds. According to BarclayHedge data, the assets under management (AUM) of managed futures funds stood at USD 340340 billion at the end of 20242024. A sizeable additional allocation runs through quantitative investment strategies (QIS) offered and executed by major investment banks.

Lintner (1983) provided the first evidence that managed futures deliver better risk-adjusted returns and offer strong diversification benefits for long-only portfolios. Subsequent studies (see, among others, Hamill et al (2016), Dao et al (2017), Harvey et al (2019), Sepp and Dezeraud (2019), and Sepp (2020)) reinforce the diversification role of managed futures, so many private and institutional portfolios now carry some exposure to them.

Some large fund managers publish research papers on the analysis of their models, including Hurst et al (2013) at AQR, Baz et al (2015) at Man Group, and Dao et al (2017) at Capital Fund Management. Replicating an industry benchmark such as the SG Trend Index is reasonably straightforward, as we show in Section 7, and managers pursue outperformance through second-order proprietary features, including style factors, risk management, and other risk premia (Carver, 2023).

On the modeling side, the profitability of trend-following (TF) systems connects to the return-predictability literature in financial economics: Pesaran and Timmermann (1995) document the economic significance of stock-return predictability, Cooper et al (2004) document the dependence of momentum profits on the market state, and Bottazzi et al (2019) derive short-term momentum and long-term reversal in equilibrium, which gives an economic origin for the serial dependence that we take as exogenous.

From a purely theoretical viewpoint, serial dependence under the statistical measure is not inconsistent with the absence of arbitrage: by the Dalang–Morton–Willinger theorem (Dalang et al, 1990), the absence of arbitrage in discrete time is equivalent to the existence of an equivalent martingale measure. Under that measure and the appropriate integrability conditions, the discounted price process has uncorrelated increments, which in general is not the case under the physical measure. Furthermore, the asset drift under the two measures can differ substantially. Our net Sharpe ratio analysis sharpens the point quantitatively: at the empirically observed first-lag autocorrelations, the proxy break-even cost in equation (6.13) lies below realistic trading costs, so the short-memory predictability is not exploitable net of frictions.

This paper provides methodological and practical results on TF systems. We unify three approaches to the construction of TF systems, which we term European, American, and Time Series Momentum (TSMOM) systems, and we find a set of parameters for which the three systems are strongly correlated and generate similar performance to the SG Trend Index. In the theoretical part, we link the expected return of the European TF system to the autocorrelation function and drift of a generic process driving the dynamics of returns. In related analysis, Dao et al (2017) show that the performance of the risk-managed trend system is given as a difference between a long-term variance and a short-term variance of the returns of the underlying instrument. This difference-of-variances decomposition originates with Bruder and Gaussel (2011), and our sample-path identity gives its exact EWMA-weighted sample form with the explicit boundary term. Quantitative aspects of TF systems in the Gaussian framework are studied by Grebenkov and Serror (2014), Ferreira et al (2018), Zakamulin and Giner (2020), Valeyre (2025). Jusselin et al (2017) derive the mean, the variance, and the skewness of EWMA trend following under trend-plus-noise dynamics, and Martin and Bana (2012) compute moments of linear momentum strategies under Gaussian dynamics. Martin (2023) derives the term structure of the skewness of momentum trading returns in closed form, and treats the expected return by simulation. In the cross-section, Lo and MacKinlay (1990) decompose trading profits into weighted autocovariances and a squared-mean term. Goulding et al (2023) and Moreira and Muir (2017) attribute the alpha of a risk-scaled strategy to the covariance between the risk signal and future returns.

We instead decompose the return of the raw signal into an autocorrelation term and a drift term, before any risk scaling. We extend the available results to derive an exact analytical formula linking the performance of the TF system to the autocorrelation of the volatility-normalized returns under generic processes. We show that the TF system is expected to be profitable when the autocorrelation of returns is positive even if the drift is zero. We also show that the TF system is expected to be profitable for any process with a large positive or negative drift if the filter span is large. We derive a closed-form proxy for the expected volatility-normalized turnover of the European TF system, exact for the signal component under independent Gaussian returns. Further, we derive the Sharpe ratio of the European TF system in closed form, using the Isserlis theorem for the variance of its daily returns. To our knowledge, the closed-form Sharpe ratio linking the risk-adjusted performance of a TF system to the autocorrelation function of the volatility-normalized returns is new. The two results hold at two levels of generality. The expected-return formula requires only a stationary mean, variance, and autocorrelation function, so it holds for any stationary autocorrelation function. The Sharpe ratio additionally assumes a causal linear process with independent innovations, which fixes the fourth-moment structure. The generating function admits a spectral representation in which the span selects the bandwidth of a Poisson kernel applied to the spectrum of the volatility-normalized returns (Section 5).

We illustrate the analytical results under white noise, AR-1, and fractional ARFIMA processes. The ARFIMA process carries both short-term and long-term mean reversion and trend features, and it extends the moving-average analysis of Brock et al (1992). In the empirical part, we apply the systems to liquid futures contracts and verify the analytical Sharpe ratios against the backtests. The scope of the present paper is the second and third moments of the strategy: the expected return, the variance, the gross and net Sharpe ratios, and, under white noise, the skewness of the aggregated returns, whose term structure Martin (2023) derives in closed form for linear systems and which we obtain within our unified framework and take to the futures data. The convexity profile of TF overlays and the diversification benefits for long-only portfolios are analyzed in a companion paper.

Compared to the cited results, our contributions are the exact sample-path identity for the cumulative return and the closed-form solution for the gross Sharpe ratio under a generic stationary autocorrelation function within the linear-process class, including the long-short filter, together with the closed-form skewness of the aggregated returns under white noise. We further derive the leading-order net Sharpe ratio under proportional trading costs, with a closed-form break-even cost for short-memory dynamics and a power-law optimal span under long memory. We validate the formula on market data: in an in-sample reconstruction, the sample autocorrelation functions of 8484 futures contracts reproduce the realized Sharpe ratios with a pooled correlation of 0.990.99 and a regression slope of 0.960.96 (Section 7.3).

Our analysis complements the optimal-control strand of trend following. Dai et al (2010) derive the optimal trading rule for a trend follower under a continuous-time regime-switching model, solving an optimal stopping problem for the entry and exit times. We take the trading rules as given by industry practice and characterize their performance analytically, so our evaluation results complement the optimal-design strand.

Our paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the framework and necessary tools for the construction of TF systems. In Section 3, we introduce the three approaches for building TF systems. In Section 4, we develop the European TF system and derive key analytical results. In Section 5, we derive the closed-form Sharpe ratio of the European TF system. In Section 6, we analyze the expected return and the Sharpe ratio of the European TF system under specific return-generating processes. In Section 7, we apply the TF systems considered to real-world data of liquid futures and consider several implementation aspects. All proofs and auxiliary results are provided in the appendices.

2 Framework and Necessary Tools

The underlying instruments of most TF systems are futures. Futures markets provide leveraged exposure to equity indices, government bonds, foreign exchange (FX) rates, and commodities. Since futures contracts have set expiration dates, existing positions must be rolled over. Continuous time series of futures prices (termed as continuous futures) for historical analysis are obtained by stitching the front and second contracts at roll events, which occur at some time prior to the first notice day of the contract. The stitching adjusts the price level at each roll, so the relative returns of the continuous series carry no roll-related jumps and equal the excess returns of the held contract (Carver, 2023). We assume that the base currency for all systems is the United States Dollar (USD).

Definition 2.1 (Futures markets and their returns).

We consider the set {t}\{t\} of observation times (without loss of generality, we assume weekday observations) and the set {st}\{s_{t}\} of sample prices of continuous futures incorporating excess USD returns. We define the lag-1 difference dtd_{t} as follows:

dt=st−st−1,d_{t}=s_{t}-s_{t-1}, (2.1)

and the relative return rtr_{t} as follows:

rt=st/st−1−1.r_{t}=s_{t}/s_{t-1}-1. (2.2)

We convert the daily return of a non-USD contract to USD by the most common futures convention, in which the local return is scaled by the FX ratio:

rt=(st∗/st−1∗−1)​(xt/xt−1),r_{t}=\left(s^{*}_{t}/s^{*}_{t-1}-1\right)\left(x_{t}/x_{t-1}\right), (2.3)

where st∗s^{*}_{t} is the local price and xtx_{t} is the exchange rate of the local currency X to USD. Returns on futures contracts are excess returns, because futures margins are small and funding costs are embedded into futures returns by arbitrage.

2.1 EWMA Filter

The design of TF systems is typically based on inference of trend indicators from noisy price and returns data. One of the most commonly used filters for the design of TF systems is the exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) filter.

We consider a stochastic process yty_{t} on the grid of discrete observation times {t}\{t\} with ordered sequence {yt}\{y_{t}\}. In our context, {yt}\{y_{t}\} represents the realizations of the price or returns of a financial instrument, such as a financial future contract. We introduce the statistical measure ℙ\mathbb{P} for computing population moments of {yt}\{y_{t}\}.

Definition 2.2 (EWMA Filter, Holt (1957)).

The exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) filter with smoothing parameter ν\nu, 0<ν<10<\nu<1, on sequence {yt}\{y_{t}\} is defined as:

ℒ(ν)​(yt)≡(1−ν)​(yt+ν1​yt−1+ν2​yt−2+…)=(1−ν)​∑m=0∞νm​yt−m=(1−ν)​yt+ν​ℒ(ν)​(yt−1).\begin{split}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(y_{t})&\equiv\left(1-\nu\right)\left(y_{t}+\nu^{1}y_{t-1}+\nu^{2}y_{t-2}+...\right)\\ &=\left(1-\nu\right)\sum^{\infty}_{m=0}\nu^{m}y_{t-m}\\ &=\left(1-\nu\right)y_{t}+\nu\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(y_{t-1}).\end{split} (2.4)

The smoothing parameter can be specified in terms of the span period as follows:

ν=1−2span+1,\nu=1-\frac{2}{\mathrm{span}+1}, (2.5)

where span\mathrm{span} is the lookback period of the EWMA filter measured in units of observation times.

The EWMA filter in equation (2.4) for serially independent variables {yt}\{y_{t}\} can be interpreted as an estimator of the running mean with the following variance:

Var⁡[ℒ(ν)​(yn)]≡1−ν1+ν​ϑ0=1span​ϑ0.\Var\left[\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(y_{n})\right]\equiv\frac{1-\nu}{1+\nu}\vartheta_{0}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{span}}\vartheta_{0}. (2.6)

Thus, for serially independent data, the EWMA filter reduces the variance as much as the moving-average (MA) filter with the window equal to the span.

Definition 2.3 (Variance-preserving EWMA filter).

We define the adjusted filter:

ℒ~(ν)​(yt)=1+ν1−ν​ℒ(ν)​(yt).\tilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(\nu)}(y_{t})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\nu}{1-\nu}}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(y_{t}). (2.7)
Proposition 2.4.

Let {yt}\{y_{t}\} be serially independent under ℙ\mathbb{P} with variance Var⁡[yt]=ϑ0\Var[y_{t}]=\vartheta_{0}. The variance-preserving filter in equation (2.7) satisfies:

Var⁡[ℒ~(ν)​(yt)]=ϑ0.\Var[\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(\nu)}(y_{t})]=\vartheta_{0}. (2.8)

The proof is provided in Appendix B.1.

Finally, we introduce the long-short EWMA filter, termed a double filter by Martin and Bana (2012) and Martin (2023).

Definition 2.5 (Variance-preserving long-short filter).

We define the long-short EWMA filter as follows:

ℒ​𝒮~(ν1,ν2)​(yn)≡l~1​ℒ~(ν1)​(yn)−l~2​ℒ~(ν2)​(yn)=l~1​1+ν11−ν1​ℒ(ν1)​(yn)−l~2​1+ν21−ν2​ℒ(ν2)​(yn)≡l1​ℒ(ν1)​(yn)−l2​ℒ(ν2)​(yn),\begin{split}\widetilde{\mathcal{LS}}^{(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})}(y_{n})&\equiv\widetilde{l}_{1}\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(\nu_{1})}(y_{n})-\widetilde{l}_{2}\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(\nu_{2})}(y_{n})\\ &=\widetilde{l}_{1}\sqrt{\frac{1+\nu_{1}}{1-\nu_{1}}}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{1})}(y_{n})-\widetilde{l}_{2}\sqrt{\frac{1+\nu_{2}}{1-\nu_{2}}}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{2})}(y_{n})\\ &\equiv l_{1}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{1})}(y_{n})-l_{2}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{2})}(y_{n}),\end{split} (2.9)

2.2 Volatility Estimation and Volatility-Normalized Returns

Volatility is the key input for position sizing. Most often, it is estimated with the EWMA filter without mean adjustment, applied to the price changes in equation (2.1):

σtp​r​i​c​e=ℒ(νσ)​(dt2),\sigma^{price}_{t}=\sqrt{\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{\sigma})}\left(d^{2}_{t}\right)}, (2.12)

or for relative returns in equation (2.2) by:

σtr​e​t​u​r​n=ℒ(νσ)​(rt2),\sigma^{return}_{t}=\sqrt{\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{\sigma})}\left(r^{2}_{t}\right)}, (2.13)

where νσ\nu_{\sigma} is the corresponding smoothing parameter.

The American TF system measures volatility by the average true range (ATR) of daily prices, which we define in Appendix A. The ATR-based estimates are highly correlated with the standard deviations of returns, with an average R2R^{2} of 90%90\% across our core futures contracts, so both risk measures lead to similar system behavior.

We compute the volatility-normalized daily returns ztz_{t} as follows:

zt=rtσt−1,z_{t}=\frac{r_{t}}{\sigma_{t-1}}, (2.14)

where σt−1\sigma_{t-1} is lag-1 volatility of daily returns.

The returns ztz_{t} can be interpreted as the returns of a strategy with volatility targeting in equation (4.2) with σtarget=a\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}=\sqrt{a}. Empirically, the realized variance of ztz_{t} is close to one when the lagged volatility estimator is well calibrated, sufficiently stable, and tracks the conditional second moment of the returns. For S&P 500 index futures, the EWMA volatility averages 17%17\%, the volatility-target weight from equation (4.2) with σtarget=15%\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}=15\% averages 1.091.09, and the volatility-normalized returns from equation (2.14) have a standard deviation of 0.960.96.

3 Trend-Following Systems

We differentiate between three approaches for signal generation of TF systems, based on our experience and communications with CTA managers.

Definition 3.1 (Trend-following systems).

1. European TF system is based on continuous weights computed using the EWMA filter (other filters can also be applied) as in equations (4.1) and (4.2). This approach is formulated by a number of large European CTA managers (see Dao et al (2017) and Baz et al (2015)). European systems assume continuous position sizes proportional to the signal strength, so the number of contracts fluctuates day-to-day, up to discretization given contract sizes.

2. American TF originates from early adopters of CTAs in North America11 1 The labels European and American follow industry usage and do not refer to option exercise styles. The European system updates the position continuously, and the American system trades at discrete breakout and stop levels., in particular, from the so-called turtle traders in the 1980s (Covel, 2009, Faith, 2007). Channel and breakout systems are tested by Lukac et al (1988) and Szakmary et al (2010), Park and Irwin (2007) survey technical trading rules, Kaminski and Lo (2014) analyze the stop-loss exit leg, and Levine and Pedersen (2016) and Brock et al (1992) study moving-average crossover rules. We generalize this approach in Definition A.3 following the design of the turtle systems. The American system trades break-outs from ranges with binary position sizes, so the exposure is fully allocated when the signal is on and zero otherwise.

3. Time Series Momentum (TSMOM) TF system is based on the price momentum as in equation (A.15) or, more generally, on the momentum of the returns adjusted for volatility as in equation (A.16). This approach is commonly used in academic studies (see Moskowitz et al (2012), Hurst et al (2013), Baltas (2015), and Dudler et al (2015)). The rebalancing frequency is typically monthly in the cited literature. In equation (A.16), the frequency is set by the period length LL in days, and in practice we recommend weekly to monthly rebalancing with L∈(5,30)L\in(5,30).

Although the three systems generate trend-following signals differently, Section 7.2 finds parameter specifications under which they deliver similar risk-adjusted performances and closely correlated returns, matching CTA benchmarks such as the SG Trend Index.

3.1 European TF System

Our approach to generate the trend-following signal is close to that of Dao et al (2017) who specify the allocation to each contract by:

wt=1σt​ℒ(ν)​(dtσt−1),w_{t}=\frac{1}{\sigma_{t}}\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}\left(\frac{d_{t}}{\sigma_{t-1}}\right), (3.1)

where ℒ(ν)\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)} is the EWMA operator defined in equation (2.4), σt\sigma_{t} is the volatility estimated using the EWMA filter in equation (2.12). We differ by using relative returns for the volatility in equation (2.13) and volatility-normalized returns for the signal, with the full construction in Definition 4.1. The meta-parameters are the smoothing value ν\nu of the long filter or the pair (ν1,ν2)(\nu_{1},\nu_{2}) of a long-short filter.

3.2 American and TSMOM TF Systems

The American TF system generates discrete long and short positions from the crossover of two EWMA filters applied to futures prices. The entry rules apply a signal buffer, and the exit rules apply trailing stop-losses, with both scaled by the ATR of daily prices. Position sizes are binary and fixed at trade inception, so the system trades at discrete breakout and stop levels. We define the system in Appendix A.

The TSMOM system sizes positions by the momentum of past returns, following Moskowitz et al (2012). We generalize the signal to the normalized sum of the signs of volatility-normalized returns over MM periods of LL days each, mirroring the European signal. We define the system in Appendix A.

The three systems monetize the same underlying trend signal, and Section 7.2 documents their strong pairwise correlations and their 80%80\% average correlation with the SG Trend Index. We focus the analysis on the European system, because its continuous signal admits exact closed-form results, and Section 7.3 shows empirically that the European closed form ranks the realized performance of the American and TSMOM implementations.

4 Construction of European TF System

Definition 4.1 (European TF system).
  1. 1.

    We consider the sequence of daily returns {rt}\{r_{t}\} of a continuous futures contract. We introduce an estimator for the daily (non-annualized) volatility of the daily returns that produces a sequence of estimated volatilities {σt}\{\sigma_{t}\} of daily returns. We use volatility-normalized daily returns ztz_{t} as computed in equation (2.14).

  2. 2.

    The signal StS_{t} is computed using either the variance-preserving EWMA filter in equation (2.7) or the long-short filter in equation (2.9) as follows:

    St=ℒ~(ν)​(zt),St=ℒ​𝒮~(ν1,ν2)​(zt).S_{t}=\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{(\nu)}(z_{t}),\ S_{t}=\widetilde{\mathcal{LS}}^{(\nu_{1},\nu_{2})}(z_{t}). (4.1)
  3. 3.

    The position size (or the position weight per trade level) is linearly proportional to the signal StS_{t} and to the volatility-target weight wtv​tw^{vt}_{t} as follows:

    wt=St​wtv​t,wtv​t=σtargeta​σt,w_{t}=S_{t}w^{vt}_{t},\ w^{vt}_{t}=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sqrt{a}\sigma_{t}}, (4.2)

    where σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}} is the annualized volatility target and aa is the annualization factor (a=260a=260 for daily returns, the weekday count of Definition 2.1).

We stress that the goal of targeting volatility in equation (4.2) is not risk management. Instead, we seek volatility-normalized returns for signal generation and for the performance of the TF system on the instrument level.

Corollary 4.2 (Daily return of European TF system).

Using equation (4.2) for computing the end-of-day weights of the European TF system, the daily return of the system for each instrument is computed by22 2 We assume end-of-day rebalancing at the close. In practice, orders are sampled and submitted shortly before the session close.:

ft≡wt−1​rt=St−1​σtargeta​σt−1​rt=σtargeta​St−1​zt.f_{t}\equiv w_{t-1}r_{t}=S_{t-1}\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sqrt{a}\sigma_{t-1}}r_{t}=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sqrt{a}}S_{t-1}z_{t}. (4.3)

As a result, the day-tt return of the trend-following strategy is proportional to the volatility-normalized return weighted by the signal observed on the previous day, so the daily return is a path-dependent function of the past volatility-normalized returns.

In the idealized model in which the volatility-normalized returns are independent with zero mean and unit variance and the volatility denominator is treated as fixed, the variance-preserving signal has unit variance at every signal span, and the strategy variance equals σtarget2/a\sigma^{2}_{\mathrm{target}}/a. With an estimated volatility, the variance of ztz_{t} and of the weights depends on the span of the volatility estimator, so the invariance is approximate. The long-term volatility of the trend-following system is then close to σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}.

In Figure 4.1, we illustrate the European TF system on the S&P 500 index future for fast, medium, and slow long-short EWMA filters. The standard deviation of all three filters is close to one in panel (A). The average weights in panel (B) are positive, reflecting the positive long-term drift of the index, and the weights become extreme during periods of low realized volatility, which CTA managers mitigate with floors in practice. The realized volatility of daily returns on the TF system in panel (C) is 18%18\% on average, close to the 15%15\% target.

4.1 Connection to Merton Problem and Kelly Sizing

The connection between the position sizing of the European TF system in equation (4.2) and the Merton problem for the optimization of long-term portfolio growth (Merton, 1969) offers a useful interpretation. Practitioners describe volatility targeting as fractional Kelly sizing (Carver, 2023), and we make the link explicit. Watt (2026) revisits the discrete-time growth-optimal allocation over one risky and one risk-free asset, which is the setting of our daily grid with excess returns.

Returns on futures contracts are excess returns, so the Kelly rule of Merton (1969), w∗=μ~/σ2w^{*}=\tilde{\mu}/\sigma^{2}, becomes w∗=(μ~/σ)×(1/σ)w^{*}=\left(\tilde{\mu}/\sigma\right)\times\left(1/\sigma\right), where the first term is the Sharpe ratio of the continuous futures and the second term is the volatility sizing. Volatilities and Sharpe ratios are time-inhomogeneous and cyclical, so we replace the two terms with their rolling estimates, w^t∗=S​R^t/σ^t\widehat{w}^{*}_{t}=\widehat{SR}_{t}/\widehat{\sigma}_{t}. The weight of the European TF system in equation (4.2) has this form up to the filter loading, because the EWMA filter of the volatility-normalized returns estimates the Sharpe ratio, S​R^t=ℒ(ν)​(zt)\widehat{SR}_{t}=\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(z_{t}). The variance-preserving filter applies the loading l=spanl=\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}, so the weight is a span-dependent multiple of the Kelly fraction. The Kelly rule also assumes independent returns, while we apply the filter to serially dependent returns. For the white noise model with drift, equation (6.3) gives the expected annual return of the TF system proportional to the square of the annualized drift, which is in line with the expected growth rate of one-half of the squared Sharpe ratio in the continuous-time Merton solution.

4.2 Cumulative Return of European TF System

By construction, the daily return of the European TF system is given in equation (4.3). For generality, we consider the linear scaling of the EWMA filter for signal generation in equation (4.1):

ℒ(ν,l)​(zt)≡l​ℒ(ν)​(zt),\mathcal{L}^{(\nu,l)}(z_{t})\equiv l\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(z_{t}), (4.4)

4.3 Cumulative Return through Sample Autocorrelation

We introduce the sample autocorrelation of volatility-normalized returns {zt}\{z_{t}\} realized over the period TT as follows:

ρ^T​(m)=γ^T​(m)γ^T​(0),γ^T​(0)=1T​∑t=1T(zt−z¯T)2,γ^T​(m)=1T​∑t=1T(zt−z¯T)​(zt−m−z¯T).\begin{split}\hat{\rho}_{T}(m)&=\frac{\hat{\gamma}_{T}(m)}{\hat{\gamma}_{T}(0)},\\ \hat{\gamma}_{T}(0)&=\frac{1}{T}\sum^{T}_{t=1}\left(z_{t}-\overline{z}_{T}\right)^{2},\\ \hat{\gamma}_{T}(m)&=\frac{1}{T}\sum^{T}_{t=1}\left(z_{t}-\overline{z}_{T}\right)\left(z_{t-m}-\overline{z}_{T}\right).\end{split} (4.12)

Two conventions and one boundary term make the identity in Proposition 4.3 exact. Second, the estimator γ^T​(m)\hat{\gamma}_{T}(m) in equation (4.12) sums over t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T and uses the pre-sample observations, while the conventional estimator sums over t=m+1,…,Tt=m+1,\ldots,T, and the ratio ρ^T​(m)\hat{\rho}_{T}(m) normalizes by γ^T​(0)\hat{\gamma}_{T}(0) alone, so it is an identity-specific lag product and need not lie in [−1,1][-1,1]. Third, the boundary term RTR_{T} collects the cross products of the sample mean with the shifted windows, because the sample mean centers the window t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T and not its lagged copies, and it vanishes when z¯T=0\overline{z}_{T}=0. Under Assumption 4.8, 𝔼​|Δm|\mathbb{E}\left|\Delta_{m}\right| grows at most linearly in mm, so RTR_{T} is of the order span/T\mathrm{span}/T in expected magnitude relative to E⁡(T)E(T) at a nonzero expected return, and the centered decomposition without RTR_{T} is an approximation for T≫spanT\gg\mathrm{span}. Truncating the filter at the sample start adds a separate term of the same order. The population statement in Corollary 4.9 is free of all three effects under Assumption 4.8.

4.4 Turnover Analysis

The average volatilities of futures returns range from 2%2\% for short rates to above 30%30\% for most commodities, so, after volatility-normalized position sizing, the realized turnover of managed futures programs may be dominated by a few low-volatility contracts with inflated notional exposures. We introduce the volatility-normalized turnover UtU_{t} as a stable measure of the turnover of futures contracts.

Definition 4.5 (Volatility-normalized turnover).

We define UtU_{t} as follows:

Ut≡a​σt​|wt−wt−1|,U_{t}\equiv\sqrt{a}\sigma_{t}\left|w_{t}-w_{t-1}\right|, (4.15)

where σt\sigma_{t} is the volatility of daily returns and aa is the annualization factor.

Proposition 4.6.

Assuming serially independent Gaussian ztz_{t} with unit variance ϑ0=1\vartheta_{0}=1 and the specification of the weight in equation (4.2) for the European TF system with the variance-preserving EWMA filter in equation (2.7), the expected annualized signal turnover Ut(s​i​g​n​a​l)=σtarget​|St−St−1|U^{(signal)}_{t}=\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}\left|S_{t}-S_{t-1}\right| is given by:

𝔼⁡[a​Ut(s​i​g​n​a​l)]=2​aπ​σtarget​1−ν.\mathbb{E}\left[aU^{(signal)}_{t}\right]=\frac{2a}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}\sqrt{1-\nu}. (4.16)

For the European TF system, the leading order of the expected turnover is inversely proportional to the square root of the EWMA filter span. The formula is free of process parameters only under the independence assumption, because the variance of the signal increment loads on the autocorrelation function when the returns are serially dependent. The full turnover UtU_{t} in equation (4.15) contains both the signal-increment and the volatility-update components, which the absolute value does not separate additively, so the closed forms serve as the independence-based signal-turnover proxy for 𝔼⁡[a​Ut]\mathbb{E}[aU_{t}].

Proposition 4.7.

Assuming serially independent Gaussian ztz_{t} with unit variance ϑ0=1\vartheta_{0}=1 and the long-short EWMA filter in equation (2.9) for the specification of the weight in equation (4.2), the expected annualized signal turnover of the long-short filter is given by:

𝔼⁡[a​Ut(s​i​g​n​a​l)]=2​aπ​σtarget​ζ,\mathbb{E}\left[aU^{(signal)}_{t}\right]=\frac{2a}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}\sqrt{\zeta}, (4.17)

where ζ\zeta is given through the normalization qq of equation (2.10) by

ζ=q22​(1−ν11+ν1+1−ν21+ν2−2​(1−ν1)​(1−ν2)1−ν1​ν2).\zeta=\frac{q^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{1-\nu_{1}}{1+\nu_{1}}+\frac{1-\nu_{2}}{1+\nu_{2}}-\frac{2\left(1-\nu_{1}\right)\left(1-\nu_{2}\right)}{1-\nu_{1}\nu_{2}}\right).

Proofs are given in Appendix B.4 and B.5. The closed forms are exact for the signal turnover under the stated assumptions and serve as leading-order proxies for the full turnover. The derivation retains the signal-increment component, omits the volatility-update component, and applies the Gaussian mean-absolute-value formula to the signed signal increment, which is exact for Gaussian innovations. Across the white-noise, AR-1, and ARFIMA exhibits, the proxy stays within 8.4%8.4\% of the signal-level MC turnover, with the largest gap at the shortest span, and the residual gap arises from the serial dependence, the non-Gaussianity, and the volatility-normalization pipeline. Within the full pipeline at the volatility span of 3333 days, the single-filter turnover exceeds the proxy by about 4%4\%. For the long-short filter, the small signal increment amplifies the volatility-update term, and the proxy understates the pipeline turnover by a factor of 1.61.6 to 2.32.3 across our processes, and by at most 29%29\% at the volatility span of 250250 days (Section 6.4).

At the spans of the empirical section, the signal-turnover proxy gives 393%393\% per year for the single 250-day filter and 88%88\% for LS(250,20), which is a significant reduction for paractical purposes, because the two legs carry the identical loading qq on the contemporaneous innovation, which cancels exactly in the signal increment.

4.5 Expected Cumulative Return

We state the assumption on the volatility-normalized returns that underlies our analytical population-based results on the performance of the European TF system.

Assumption 4.8 (Characteristics of volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t}).

We consider the volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t} in equation (2.14) with the following population-based characteristics for the expected mean, the variance, and the autocorrelation function, respectively, under statistical measure ℙ\mathbb{P}:

𝔼ℙ​[zt]=μ,Varℙ⁡[zt]=ϑ>0,𝔼ℙ[1ϑ(zt−μ)(zt−m−μ)]=ρ(m),m=1,2,….\begin{split}&\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\left[z_{t}\right]=\mu,\\ &\Var^{\mathbb{P}}\left[z_{t}\right]=\vartheta>0,\\ &\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}\left[\frac{1}{\vartheta}(z_{t}-\mu)(z_{t-m}-\mu)\right]=\rho(m),\ m=1,2,\ldots.\end{split} (4.18)

We set ρ⁡(0)=1\rho(0)=1, extending the autocorrelation function to the zero lag.

Assumption 4.8 requires no specification of the raw returns rtr_{t}, because the systems trade the volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t} and every population formula depends on the process only through the moments of ztz_{t}. When the volatility is constant, the autocorrelation functions of ztz_{t} and rtr_{t} coincide, and the annualized mean of ztz_{t} equals the annualized Sharpe ratio of the instrument. More generally, if rt=σt−1​xtr_{t}=\sigma_{t-1}x_{t} with a standardized stationary process xtx_{t} independent of the predictable volatility, then ρr​(m)=ρx​(m)​𝔼​[σt​σt−m]/𝔼⁡[σt2]\rho_{r}(m)=\rho_{x}(m)\,\mathbb{E}[\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t-m}]/\mathbb{E}[\sigma^{2}_{t}], so time-varying volatility dampens the autocorrelation of the raw returns, and the normalization recovers it. Under the estimated EWMA volatility, the normalization keeps ztz_{t} close to a stationary process with unit variance, and its autocorrelation is a dampened version of the raw-return autocorrelation, which Section 6.4 quantifies. The empirical inputs of Section 7.3 are estimated directly from ztz_{t}, so the formulas are applied to the process that they assume.

5 Sharpe Ratio of European TF System

Corollary 4.9 of Section 4 links the expected return of the European TF system to the autocorrelation function and the drift of the volatility-normalized returns. The expected return alone, however, cannot rank filter spans, because the risk of the strategy changes with the span as well. In this section, we derive the variance of the daily strategy return in closed form and obtain the annualized Sharpe ratio. We define the annualized gross Sharpe ratio33 3 The daily returns ftf_{t} are serially dependent because the signal is persistent. We define the annualized Sharpe ratio on the moments of daily returns, which is the convention of our backtests and of industry reporting for liquid managed futures. The horizon-based Sharpe ratio of Lo (2002), defined on the variance of aggregated returns, differs from our definition when returns are autocorrelated. Under the white noise with zero mean assumption, the covariances of daily strategy returns vanish at all lags and the two definitions coincide. For persistent signals, the daily strategy returns are typically positively autocorrelated, so the daily-moment annualization overstates the horizon-based Sharpe ratio. of a strategy with daily returns ftf_{t} as

S​R=a​𝔼ℙ​[ft]Varℙ⁡[ft],SR=\sqrt{a}\,\frac{\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}]}{\sqrt{\Var^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}]}}, (5.1)

where aa is the number of trading days per year, and 𝔼ℙ​[ft]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}] and Varℙ⁡[ft]\Var^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}] are the mean and the variance of the daily returns under ℙ\mathbb{P}. Returns on futures contracts are excess returns, so we do not subtract a risk-free rate. The daily return in equation (4.5) is a product of the volatility-normalized return ztz_{t} and the lagged filter value, and both variables are linear in past returns. The variance of such a product is available in closed form through an extension of the Isserlis theorem. As a result, the Sharpe ratio depends on the autocorrelation moments of the returns and on the excess kurtosis of the innovations.

The gross Sharpe ratio excludes trading costs. We define the net Sharpe ratio under a proportional cost cc per unit of the volatility-normalized turnover UtU_{t} in equation (4.15):

S​Rn​e​t=a​𝔼ℙ​[ft]−c​𝔼ℙ​[Ut]Varℙ⁡[ft]=S​R−c​𝔼ℙ​[a​Ut]a​Varℙ⁡[ft].SR^{net}=\sqrt{a}\,\frac{\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}]-c\,\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[U_{t}]}{\sqrt{\Var^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}]}}=SR-c\,\frac{\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{P}}[aU_{t}]}{\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{\Var^{\mathbb{P}}[f_{t}]}}. (5.2)

The second form divides the expected annual cost by the annualized volatility of the strategy. The denominator keeps the gross volatility, so the ratio is a cost-adjusted gross-risk ratio rather than the Sharpe ratio of the net return ft−c​Utf_{t}-c\,U_{t}, whose variance adds the covariance term −2​c​Cov⁡[ft,Ut]-2c\,\Cov[f_{t},U_{t}] of the first order in cc and the term c2​Var⁡[Ut]c^{2}\Var[U_{t}] of the second order. The turnover input applies the signal-turnover proxy of Propositions 4.6 and 4.7: the independence-based Gaussian closed form for the signal component of the turnover. Serial dependence changes the signal turnover itself, and the full turnover contains the volatility-update component as well, so the net results are leading-order approximations under Assumption 4.8, while the gross results are exact. We refer to the resulting closed forms as the net Sharpe ratio under the signal-turnover proxy, and we write them with the approximation sign. The net Sharpe ratio remains independent of the volatility target, because the turnover and the strategy returns are both proportional to σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}.

5.1 Autocorrelation Generating Function

Under Assumption 4.8, we define the autocorrelation generating function Φν\Phi_{\nu} and its centered version Ψν\Psi_{\nu} as follows:

Φν=∑m=0∞νm​ρ​(m),Ψν=Φν−1=∑m=1∞νm​ρ​(m).\Phi_{\nu}=\sum^{\infty}_{m=0}\nu^{m}\rho(m),\qquad\Psi_{\nu}=\Phi_{\nu}-1=\sum^{\infty}_{m=1}\nu^{m}\rho(m). (5.3)

In this notation, the autocorrelation term in the expected return in equation (4.22) equals Ψν\Psi_{\nu}: zero for white noise and ν​ϕ/(1−ν​ϕ)\nu\phi/(1-\nu\phi) for the AR-1 process. For ARFIMA processes, we evaluate Ψν\Psi_{\nu} numerically from the autocorrelation function in equations (6.16) and (6.18) truncated at 20002000 lags, where the weights νm\nu^{m} bound the truncation remainder relative to Ψν\Psi_{\nu} below 10−410^{-4} at the longest span for the fractional orders d≤0.1d\leq 0.1 used in this paper.

The generating function admits a spectral representation. By the Herglotz theorem, the autocorrelation function of any stationary process is the Fourier coefficient sequence of a normalized spectral measure FF on [−π,π][-\pi,\pi], which requires only the positive definiteness of the autocorrelation function, and the symmetrized sum gives:

2​Φν−1=∫−ππ1−ν21−2​ν​cos⁡λ+ν2​𝑑F​(λ),2\Phi_{\nu}-1=\int^{\pi}_{-\pi}\frac{1-\nu^{2}}{1-2\nu\cos\lambda+\nu^{2}}\,dF(\lambda), (5.4)

where the integrand is the Poisson kernel with the concentration parameter ν\nu. The expected return of the TF system is therefore a Poisson-kernel reading of the spectrum of the volatility-normalized returns. The system profits at zero drift if and only if the kernel-weighted spectral mass exceeds one, so trend-following alpha is excess spectral mass at low frequencies. The span sets the bandwidth of the kernel, so short spans read the whole spectrum while long spans read the spectral mass near zero, where the long memory resides. The long-short filter reads the spectrum through a signed contrast of two Poisson-kernel readings. The contrast is not a band-pass window, because the level signal retains a nonzero gain at frequency zero under the normalization in equation (2.10). The one-day signal increment has zero gain at frequency zero, so the increment, and not the level, acts as a band-pass difference of the two filters.

5.2 Variance of the Daily Return

The expected return in Corollary 4.9 requires only the first two moments of the process. The variance of the daily return involves fourth moments, so we need an assumption on the distribution of the volatility-normalized returns.

Assumption 5.1 (Linear process for volatility-normalized returns).

The volatility-normalized returns {zt}\{z_{t}\} satisfy Assumption 4.8 and admit a linear representation in the form of a Wold decomposition (see (Hamilton, 1994, Chapter 4)):

zt=μ+ϑ​∑s=0∞ψs​ϵt−s,∑s=0∞ψs2=1,z_{t}=\mu+\sqrt{\vartheta}\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}\psi_{s}\epsilon_{t-s},\qquad\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}\psi^{2}_{s}=1, (5.5)

where the innovations {ϵt}\{\epsilon_{t}\} are independent and identically distributed with zero mean, unit variance, zero third moment, and finite excess kurtosis κ=𝔼⁡[ϵt4]−3\kappa=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^{4}_{t}]-3.

The moving-average weights ψs\psi_{s} determine the autocorrelation function through ρ⁡(m)=∑s=0∞ψs​ψs+m\rho(m)=\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}\psi_{s}\psi_{s+m}. The assumption does not restrict the serial dependence between the signal and the return, because both variables load on the common innovations. The zero third moment removes cross terms between the drift and the squared innovations, and these terms are of the order of the drift times the skewness of the innovations. The excess kurtosis enters the variance of the strategy return through a single loading, which Proposition 5.3 defines. Jointly Gaussian returns correspond to the case κ=0\kappa=0, because a stationary Gaussian process is a linear process with Gaussian innovations44 4 The Wold decomposition separates a deterministic component, which we exclude. The processes of Section 6 are linear by construction..

Volatility normalization can remove most of the heavy tails and the asymmetry of raw returns, so the restrictions on the innovations are mild. Under GARCH-type dynamics, the EWMA variance recursion approximates the conditional variance, so the volatility-normalized returns are approximately the standardized innovations: in a GARCH(1,1) simulation with a raw excess kurtosis of 77, the pipeline ztz_{t} has an excess kurtosis of 0.060.06 and a first-lag autocorrelation below 0.0010.001. Positive excess kurtosis adds a positive term to the variance of the strategy return and reduces the absolute Sharpe ratio, lowering a positive ratio and moving a negative ratio toward zero. The expected return in Corollary 4.9 is unaffected, because the first moment is distribution-free. We quantify the impact of the full volatility-normalization pipeline, which the linear representation does not capture, in Section 6.4.

Lemma 5.2 (Variance of a product of variables linear in common innovations).

Let X=μX+∑s=0∞as​ϵt−sX=\mu_{X}+\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}a_{s}\epsilon_{t-s} and Y=μY+∑s=0∞bs​ϵt−sY=\mu_{Y}+\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}b_{s}\epsilon_{t-s} be linear in the innovations of Assumption 5.1, with variances σX2\sigma^{2}_{X} and σY2\sigma^{2}_{Y} and covariance σX​Y\sigma_{XY}. The variance of the product is given by:

Var⁡[X​Y]=σX2​σY2+σX​Y2+μX2​σY2+μY2​σX2+2​μX​μY​σX​Y+κ​∑s=0∞as2​bs2.\Var\left[XY\right]=\sigma^{2}_{X}\sigma^{2}_{Y}+\sigma^{2}_{XY}+\mu^{2}_{X}\sigma^{2}_{Y}+\mu^{2}_{Y}\sigma^{2}_{X}+2\mu_{X}\mu_{Y}\sigma_{XY}+\kappa\sum^{\infty}_{s=0}a^{2}_{s}b^{2}_{s}. (5.6)

For κ=0\kappa=0, equation (5.6) reduces to the Isserlis theorem for jointly Gaussian variables.

Proof is given in Appendix B.6.

We apply Lemma 5.2 to X=ztX=z_{t} and Y=ℒ(ν)​(zt−1)Y=\mathcal{L}^{(\nu)}(z_{t-1}), because the daily return in equation (4.5) is proportional to their product. The filter is a linear combination of past returns, so its moments follow from Assumption 4.8 by direct summation.

Corollary 5.4 (Moments and Sharpe ratio of the long-short system).

The result extends to the long-short EWMA filter in equation (2.9) by linearity, because the signal remains a linear combination of past returns. where the cross-covariance of the two filters follows by the same double-sum manipulation as in equation (B.17). 5.3 Annualized Sharpe Ratio

Corollary 5.5 (Sharpe ratio of European TF system).

Under Assumption 5.1 with ϑ=1\vartheta=1 and the annualized mean μa​nz=a​μ\mu^{z}_{an}=\sqrt{a}\mu, the annualized Sharpe ratio of the European TF system is given by:

S​R=a​Aν+(μa​nz)2/aBν+Aν2+κ​Kν+((μa​nz)2/a)​(1+Bν+2​Aν).SR=\frac{\sqrt{a}\,A_{\nu}+\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{B_{\nu}+A^{2}_{\nu}+\kappa K_{\nu}+\left(\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/a\right)\left(1+B_{\nu}+2A_{\nu}\right)}}. (5.12)

The Sharpe ratio does not depend on the volatility target σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}} and does not depend on the filter loading ll, because the factor l​σtarget/al\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}/\sqrt{a} multiplies the mean and the volatility of ftf_{t} equally. For κ=0\kappa=0, equation (5.12) gives the Sharpe ratio under jointly Gaussian returns. Dividing the proxy turnover of Proposition 4.6 by the annualized volatility of Proposition 5.3 and using the identity l​1−ν=1+νl\sqrt{1-\nu}=\sqrt{1+\nu}, the net Sharpe ratio of equation (5.2) follows at the leading order as:

S​Rn​e​t≈S​R−2​a​cπ​1−ν(1+ν)​(Bν+Aν2+κ​Kν+((μa​nz)2/a)​(1+Bν+2​Aν)).SR^{net}\approx SR-\frac{2ac}{\sqrt{\pi}}\,\frac{1-\nu}{\sqrt{(1+\nu)\left(B_{\nu}+A^{2}_{\nu}+\kappa K_{\nu}+\left(\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/a\right)\left(1+B_{\nu}+2A_{\nu}\right)\right)}}. (5.13)

Under zero-drift white noise, the bracket reduces to Bν=(1−ν)/(1+ν)B_{\nu}=(1-\nu)/(1+\nu) and the cost drag equals (2​a​c/π)​1−ν(2ac/\sqrt{\pi})\sqrt{1-\nu}. The net Sharpe ratio remains independent of σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}} and depends on the filter only through the span.

Equation (5.12) reduces the TF design problem for a single EWMA filter to the choice of the span, which can be selected from the autocorrelation structure and the excess kurtosis of the returns. The white-noise result in equation (6.4) requires no distributional assumption beyond serial independence and a finite second moment. Under white noise, ztz_{t} is independent of the signal built from zt−1,zt−2,…z_{t-1},z_{t-2},\ldots, so the variance of the product factorizes into moments of order two. For autocorrelated returns, the excess kurtosis reduces the absolute Sharpe ratio through the term κ​Kν\kappa K_{\nu} in Proposition 5.3. For the AR-1 process of Section 6, the correction is below the Monte Carlo confidence intervals in Figure 6.2.

6 Expected Return and Sharpe Ratio under Specific Processes

In this section, we apply different stochastic processes to derive analytic solutions for the expected return and the Sharpe ratio of the trend-following strategy. We also compare analytical results with estimates obtained using Monte Carlo simulations55 5 The Python package trendfollowing, which reproduces all analytical results and exhibits of this paper, is available at https://github.com/ArturSepp/TrendFollowingSystems..

For verification of analytical results, we generate 10001000 Monte Carlo paths of 5050 years of daily returns (1300013000 observations per path). We simulate the daily returns {rt}\{r_{t}\} assuming the time step d​t=1/adt=1/a, with a=260a=260, and the noise process with variance equal to d​tdt. We compute volatility-normalized returns {zt}\{z_{t}\} in equation (2.14) using the EWMA volatility estimator in equation (2.13) with span=33\mathrm{span}=3366 6 The confidence intervals improve with a longer volatility span. We use the shorter span in alignment with the implementation of TF strategies and industry practice (Dao et al (2017), Robertson (2025)). and with the volatility target σtarget=15%\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}=15\%. The processes of this section specify the raw returns with constant innovation variance, so the volatility-normalized returns inherit the autocorrelation function and the drift of the process up to the estimation effect of the volatility filter, which Section 6.4 quantifies. The gross results assume zero trading costs. For the net Sharpe ratio, we apply the cost of c=20c=20bp per unit of the volatility-normalized turnover77 7 This corresponds to about 2%2\% and 1%1\% of annual trading costs for higher and medium frequency TF systems, respectively, see Figure 7.2. to each simulated path, and we compute the net Sharpe ratio per path as the annual return minus the cost times the annualized turnover, divided by the gross annualized volatility, matching equation (5.2). For each path, we compute the average annual return to generate the sample of 10001000 MC estimates {F^1​y}\{\hat{F}_{1y}\}. The process exhibits report the mean of the per-path estimates, with the 95%95\% confidence interval 1.96×s​t​d​e​v​(F^1​y)/10001.96\times stdev(\hat{F}_{1y})/\sqrt{1000} across the paths. The verification table of Section 6.4 reports the pooled estimators over all paths, with confidence intervals from whole-path blocks.

We compute the expected return of the European TF system in Definition 4.1 as a function of the EWMA filter span in days, labeled as follows:

1​w≡5, 2​w≡10, 1​m≡21, 3​m≡63, 6​m≡125, 1​y≡250, 2​y≡500.1w\equiv 5,\ 2w\equiv 10,\ 1m\equiv 21,\ 3m\equiv 63,\ 6m\equiv 125,\ 1y\equiv 250,\ 2y\equiv 500. (6.1)

The simulated returns enter the pipeline in two roles. They feed the volatility estimator σt\sigma_{t} in equation (2.13), and they define the volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t} in equation (2.14). All performance calculations then operate on ztz_{t}, because the identity in equation (4.3) expresses the daily strategy return as ft=(σtarget/a)​St−1​ztf_{t}=(\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}/\sqrt{a})\,S_{t-1}z_{t} with the signal computed from ztz_{t}. The simulation therefore applies the strategy to the pipeline-normalized process ztz_{t}, and every performance statistic is a functional of the volatility-normalized returns. Dividing by an estimated volatility does not by itself enforce the stationarity or the population moments of Assumption 4.8, so the Monte Carlo measures the discrepancy between the pipeline process and the analytical assumptions. The analytic values in the figures and in Table 6.1 apply the population moments of rtr_{t} in place of those of ztz_{t}, which the inheritance justifies up to the estimation effect.

6.1 White Noise

We first consider a white noise process with mean μ\mu and unit annualized variance:

rt=μ+ϵt,r_{t}=\mu+\epsilon_{t}, (6.2)

where ϵt\epsilon_{t} is normal with zero mean and variance 1/a1/a, and μ=μa​nz/a\mu=\mu^{z}_{an}/a, so the volatility-normalized returns have the daily mean μa​nz/a\mu^{z}_{an}/\sqrt{a} under a constant volatility estimate, and approximately under the estimated EWMA volatility, because the random denominator changes the expectation of 1/σt−11/\sigma_{t-1}. The autocorrelation is the Kronecker delta at m=0m=0, ρ⁡(m)=δm=0\rho(m)=\delta_{m=0}, so that the expected return F¯1​y\overline{F}_{1y} in equation (4.22) becomes as follows:

F¯1​y=(l​σtargeta)​(μa​nz)2.\bar{F}_{1y}=\left(\frac{l\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sqrt{a}}\right)(\mu^{z}_{an})^{2}. (6.3)

Thus, a TF system under white noise can be profitable only if the mean μ\mu is not zero. Figure 6.1 shows the expected return in panel (A) from equation (6.3), the gross Sharpe ratio in panel (B) from equation (6.4), and the net Sharpe ratio at c=20c=20bp in panel (C) from equation (5.13). The zero-drift Sharpe ratio is zero at every span, and the Sharpe ratio for non-zero drift grows with the span. The analytic results are within the MC confidence intervals.

We now turn to the Sharpe ratio, shown in panel (B) of Figure 6.1. Under white noise with drift, we have Ψν=0\Psi_{\nu}=0, so Aν=0A_{\nu}=0 and Bν=(1−ν)/(1+ν)=1/spanB_{\nu}=(1-\nu)/(1+\nu)=1/\mathrm{span} using the span convention in equation (2.5). Equation (5.12) becomes:

S​R=(μa​nz)2​span/a1+((μa​nz)2/a)​(span+1)≈(μa​nz)2​spana,SR=\frac{\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}\sqrt{\mathrm{span}/a}}{\sqrt{1+\left(\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/a\right)\left(\mathrm{span}+1\right)}}\approx\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{span}}{a}}, (6.4)

where the approximation drops the term of order (μa​nz)2/a\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/a. The leading order gives a simple rule. At the one-year span with span=a\mathrm{span}=a, the Sharpe ratio of the TF system approximately equals the squared Sharpe ratio of the underlying instrument, because the exact denominator in equation (6.4) exceeds one. The net Sharpe ratio follows from equation (5.13) in closed form:

S​Rn​e​t≈(μa​nz)2​span/a−(2​a​c/π)​2/(span+1)1+((μa​nz)2/a)​(span+1)≈(μa​nz)2​spana−2​a​c​2π​span.SR^{net}\approx\frac{\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}\sqrt{\mathrm{span}/a}-\left(2ac/\sqrt{\pi}\right)\sqrt{2/(\mathrm{span}+1)}}{\sqrt{1+\left(\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}/a\right)\left(\mathrm{span}+1\right)}}\approx\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{span}}{a}}-2ac\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi\,\mathrm{span}}}. (6.5)

The drift alpha grows with span\sqrt{\mathrm{span}} while the cost drag declines with 1/span1/\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}, so, under the signal-turnover proxy, any proportional cost is beaten at a long enough span. The net Sharpe ratio in panel (C) reaches 0.250.25 at the two-year span for |μa​nz|=0.5|\mu^{z}_{an}|=0.5, and the zero-drift curve isolates the pure cost drag, which declines from 0.340.34 at the one-week span to 0.040.04 at the two-year span. In the long-span limit, the direction of the signal converges to the sign of the drift and the system converges to a buy-and-hold exposure up to a deterministic scale, so the net Sharpe ratio under the proxy approaches the absolute Sharpe ratio |μa​nz||\mu^{z}_{an}| of the underlying instrument for any proportional cost (see Remark C.3).

6.2 AR-1 process

Next, we consider the AR-1 process with |ϕ|<1|\phi|<1 and the dynamics:

rt=μ+xt,xt=ϕxt−1+ϵt,\begin{split}r_{t}&=\mu+x_{t},\qquad x_{t}=\phi x_{t-1}+\epsilon_{t},\end{split} (6.6)

where |ϕ|<1\left|\phi\right|<1, ϵt\epsilon_{t} is normal with variance 1/a1/a, and the raw drift parameter μa​n\mu_{an} sets μ=μa​n/a\mu=\mu_{an}/a outside the autoregression without the intercept amplification 1/(1−ϕ)1/(1-\phi). The stationary variance of xtx_{t} is 1/(a⁡(1−ϕ2))1/(a(1-\phi^{2})), so the normalized annualized drift is μa​nz=μa​n​1−ϕ2\mu^{z}_{an}=\mu_{an}\sqrt{1-\phi^{2}}, which equals μa​n\mu_{an} to the leading order in ϕ2\phi^{2}, a 0.1%0.1\% effect at |ϕ|=0.05|\phi|=0.05.

We recall the following features of the AR-1 process. If ϕ>0\phi>0, the volatility-normalized returns are positively autocorrelated and the markets are divergent: the volatility of aggregated returns settles above the square-root-of-time benchmark by the factor (1+ϕ)/(1−ϕ)\sqrt{(1+\phi)/(1-\phi)} at long horizons. If ϕ<0\phi<0, the volatility-normalized returns are negatively autocorrelated and the markets are mean-reverting: the aggregated volatility settles below the benchmark by the same factor.

The autocorrelation of the AR-1 process is the power function:

ρ⁡(m)=ϕm.\rho(m)=\phi^{m}. (6.7)

Thus, the expected return in equation (4.22) is given by:

F¯1​y=h1​y​[ϕ​ν1−ϕ​ν]+(l​σtargeta)​(μa​nz)2.\bar{F}_{1y}=h_{1y}\left[\frac{\phi\nu}{1-\phi\nu}\right]+\left(\frac{l\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sqrt{a}}\right)\left(\mu^{z}_{an}\right)^{2}. (6.8)

We reach two conclusions. First, the expected return at zero drift is positive for ϕ>0\phi>0, when the markets are diverging, and negative for ϕ<0\phi<0, when the markets are mean-reverting. Second, the shorter the filter span, the larger the autocorrelation contribution to the expected return. Figure 6.2 shows the analytical results and the MC confidence intervals for the zero-drift AR-1 process with ϕ={−0.05,0.05}\phi=\{-0.05,0.05\}. The gross Sharpe ratio in panel (B) is positive for ϕ=0.05\phi=0.05, negative for ϕ=−0.05\phi=-0.05, and declines in magnitude with the span. Panel (C) reports the net Sharpe ratio at c=20c=20bp. The analytical results are within the MC intervals.

Under the zero-drift AR-1 process in equation (6.6), the loadings and the Sharpe ratio of panel (B) follow from equation (5.12) in closed form for κ=0\kappa=0:

Aν=(1−ν)​ϕ1−ν​ϕ,Bν=(1−ν)​(1+ν​ϕ)(1+ν)​(1−ν​ϕ),S​R=a​AνBν+Aν2.A_{\nu}=\frac{(1-\nu)\phi}{1-\nu\phi},\qquad B_{\nu}=\frac{(1-\nu)(1+\nu\phi)}{(1+\nu)(1-\nu\phi)},\qquad SR=\frac{\sqrt{a}\,A_{\nu}}{\sqrt{B_{\nu}+A^{2}_{\nu}}}. (6.9)

The AR-1 process is the linear process with the weights ψs=1−ϕ2​ϕs\psi_{s}=\sqrt{1-\phi^{2}}\,\phi^{s}, so the kurtosis loading in equation (5.9) has the closed form:

Kν=(1−ν)2​(1−ϕ2)2(ϕ−ν)2​(ϕ41−ϕ4−2​ν​ϕ31−ν​ϕ3+ν2​ϕ21−ν2​ϕ2).K_{\nu}=\frac{(1-\nu)^{2}(1-\phi^{2})^{2}}{(\phi-\nu)^{2}}\left(\frac{\phi^{4}}{1-\phi^{4}}-\frac{2\nu\phi^{3}}{1-\nu\phi^{3}}+\frac{\nu^{2}\phi^{2}}{1-\nu^{2}\phi^{2}}\right). (6.10)

At ϕ=ν\phi=\nu, equation (6.10) is interpreted by continuity. For ϕ=0.05\phi=0.05 and κ=3\kappa=3, the correction κ​Kν\kappa K_{\nu} lowers the Sharpe ratio by at most 0.2%0.2\% in relative terms across the spans from 55 to 250250 days. We therefore evaluate the AR-1 exhibits with κ=0\kappa=0.

For a small AR-1 coefficient, the expansion in ϕ\phi yields a compact approximation:

S​R≈ϕ​a⁡(1−ν2)=2​ϕ​a​spanspan+1≈2​ϕ​aspan.SR\approx\phi\sqrt{a\left(1-\nu^{2}\right)}=\frac{2\phi\sqrt{a}\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}}{\mathrm{span}+1}\approx 2\phi\sqrt{\frac{a}{\mathrm{span}}}. (6.11)

The approximation is accurate for the parameter ranges that we consider. The net Sharpe ratio admits the same expansion:

S​Rn​e​t≈ϕ​a⁡(1−ν2)−2​a​cπ​1−ν≈2​aspan​(ϕ−c​2​aπ).SR^{net}\approx\phi\sqrt{a\left(1-\nu^{2}\right)}-\frac{2ac}{\sqrt{\pi}}\sqrt{1-\nu}\approx 2\sqrt{\frac{a}{\mathrm{span}}}\left(\phi-c\sqrt{\frac{2a}{\pi}}\right). (6.12)

Both terms decay with 1/span1/\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}, so the sign of the net Sharpe ratio is span-invariant at leading order and positive if and only if c<ϕ​π/(2​a)c<\phi\sqrt{\pi/(2a)}, which is the small-ϕ\phi form of the threshold in equation (6.13). The net Sharpe ratio reveals a knife-edge property of the AR-1 alpha. The gross Sharpe ratio and the cost drag both decline with the square root of the span, so the break-even cost is nearly span-invariant, with the closed form of Proposition C.1 and the long-span limit:

c∞∗=π2​a​ϕ1−ϕ.c^{*}_{\infty}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2a}}\,\frac{\phi}{1-\phi}. (6.13)

For ϕ=0.05\phi=0.05 and a=260a=260, the proxy break-even cost varies only between 3737bp and 4141bp across the spans from one week to two years. These values lie around the lower edge of realistic costs of 4040bp to 6060bp, and the pipeline turnover of the single filter at the volatility span of 3333 days exceeds the proxy by about 4%4\%, which places the break-even costs slightly below that range. To first order, costs determine the viability of a short-memory alpha. Near the break-even level, costs also push the cost-optimal span toward longer horizons.

Proposition C.1 derives the interior optimal span in the limit c→c∞∗c\to c^{*}_{\infty}:

span∗≈6​ϕ/(1−ϕ)+3​c/(2​c∞∗)1−c/c∞∗.\mathrm{span}^{*}\approx\frac{6\phi/(1-\phi)+3c/(2c^{*}_{\infty})}{1-c/c^{*}_{\infty}}. (6.14)

As the cost approaches the break-even level, the optimal span diverges and the attainable net Sharpe ratio declines toward zero. The optimal response to a marginally profitable short-memory alpha is therefore to trade it at ever longer spans. Equation (6.14) is asymptotic in the limit c→c∞∗c\to c^{*}_{\infty} and is not intended for quantitative use at costs well below the threshold. For such costs, the interior candidate falls below the one-week minimum of our span grid, and the optimum reverts to the corner solution at the fastest span.

The closed forms expose a fundamental trade-off in the span selection. The drift contribution to the Sharpe ratio in equation (6.4) grows with span\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}, while the short-term autocorrelation contribution in equation (6.11) decays with 1/span1/\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}. A short filter monetizes short-term autocorrelation and a long filter monetizes the drift. For processes that combine both features, the Sharpe ratio in equation (5.12) may attain its maximum at an interior span, depending on the parameter magnitudes and signs, and the formula turns the span selection into an explicit function of the process parameters.

6.3 Long-memory ARFIMA Process

Granger and Joyeux (1980) and Hosking (1981) introduce the autoregressive fractionally integrated moving-average (ARFIMA) process. Schadner and Lang (2023) estimate option-implied Hurst exponents for S&P 500 stocks and document time-varying persistence of returns, which supports long memory as a priced feature. The ARFIMA (0,d,0)(0,d,0) process is a discrete-time analog of fractional Gaussian noise, with the infinite moving-average representation:

r~t=∑j=0∞ψj​ϵt−j,ψj=Γ⁡(d+j)Γ⁡(1+j)​Γ​(d),\tilde{r}_{t}=\sum^{\infty}_{j=0}\psi_{j}\epsilon_{t-j},\ \psi_{j}=\frac{\Gamma(d+j)}{\Gamma(1+j)\Gamma(d)}, (6.15)

where {ϵt}\{\epsilon_{t}\} are independent innovations with zero mean and unit variance, Gaussian in our exhibits, and Γ⁡(x)\Gamma(x) is the Gamma function. The process is covariance stationary and invertible for −1/2<d<1/2-1/2<d<1/2, which we assume throughout. At d=0d=0, the Gamma-function representation of the weights is interpreted by its white-noise limit ψ0=1\psi_{0}=1 and ψj=0\psi_{j}=0 for j≥1j\geq 1.

The variance and autocorrelation of r~t\tilde{r}_{t} are given respectively by:

γ0r~=Γ⁡(1−2​d)(Γ⁡(1−d))2,ρkr~=Γ⁡(1−d)​Γ​(k+d)Γ⁡(d)​Γ​(k−d+1).\gamma^{\tilde{r}}_{0}=\frac{\Gamma(1-2d)}{(\Gamma(1-d))^{2}},\ \rho^{\tilde{r}}_{k}=\frac{\Gamma(1-d)\Gamma(k+d)}{\Gamma(d)\Gamma(k-d+1)}. (6.16)

Further, we consider the ARFIMA (1,d,0)(1,d,0) process, which incorporates both the short-term autocorrelation produced by the AR-1 process and the long-term autocorrelation produced by the ARFIMA (0,d,0)(0,d,0) process:

rt=μ+xt,xt=ϕ​xt−1+r~t/a,r_{t}=\mu+x_{t},\qquad x_{t}=\phi x_{t-1}+\tilde{r}_{t}/\sqrt{a}, (6.17)

ρkr=ρkr~​F⁡(1,d+k,1−d+k,ϕ)+F⁡(1,d−k,1−d−k,ϕ)−1(1−ϕ)​F​(1,1+d,1−d,ϕ),\rho^{r}_{k}=\rho^{\tilde{r}}_{k}\frac{F(1,d+k,1-d+k;\phi)+F(1,d-k,1-d-k;\phi)-1}{(1-\phi)F(1,1+d,1-d;\phi)}, (6.18)
