The AR-1 autocorrelations decay geometrically, while the long-lag ARFIMA tail decays slowly, with the positive sign for d>0d>0 and the negative sign for d<0d<0.

We evaluate the autocorrelation sums in equations (4.22) and (4.23) by direct summation using equation (6.18). For heavy-tailed innovations, the kurtosis loading KνK_{\nu} follows numerically from the moving-average weights in equation (6.15), rescaled to the unit-norm convention of Assumption 5.1. Figure 6.3 shows the expected return, the gross Sharpe ratio, and the net Sharpe ratio at c=20c=20bp for the ARFIMA process with d=0.02d=0.02 and ϕ∈{−0.05,0.0,0.05}\phi\in\{-0.05,0.0,0.05\}. The calibration matches the observed first-lag autocorrelation through ρ⁡(1)=d/(1−d)\rho(1)=d/(1-d) for the pure fractional process, with d=0.02d=0.02 at the center of the 0.010.01 to 0.040.04 range of Section 7.3. Long memory alone makes the TF system profitable, and it stays profitable under short-term mean reversion when the filter span exceeds one month.

The Sharpe ratio in panel (B) is highest at the shortest spans for the pure long-memory case. Panel (C) displays the three regimes of the cost-adjusted span selection in a single figure. For ϕ=0.05\phi=0.05, the alpha dominates the cost at every span and the net Sharpe ratio declines from 0.680.68 at the one-week span, so the fast corner remains optimal. For the pure long-memory case ϕ=0\phi=0, the net Sharpe ratio is hump-shaped with an interior maximum of 0.190.19 at the one-to-three-month spans, because the ratio of the long-memory alpha to the cost drag grows with span2​d\mathrm{span}^{2d} while both decline in the span88 8 In the large-cost limit, the optimal span scales as c1/(2​d)c^{1/(2d)} and the net-to-gross ratio at the optimum converges to 4​d/(1+2​d)4d/(1+2d) (Proposition C.2). For small dd, the limit lies beyond practical cost levels: at d=0.02d=0.02 and c=20c=20bp, the continuous-span optimum lies at 3737 days with a net-to-gross ratio of 0.610.61, against the limiting value of 0.080.08. We therefore locate the cost-optimal span from the non-asymptotic proxy objective in equation (5.13), rather than from the large-cost asymptotic law.. For ϕ=−0.05\phi=-0.05, the net Sharpe ratio turns positive between the three-month and the six-month spans, so short-term mean reversion and costs together push the viable region into slow spans.

For ϕ≠0\phi\neq 0, the moving-average weights entering the kurtosis loading KνK_{\nu} are the convolution hj=∑k=0jϕk​ψj−kh_{j}=\sum^{j}_{k=0}\phi^{k}\psi_{j-k} of the fractional weights with the AR weights, normalized to unit variance. For the pure fractional process ARFIMA(0,d,0)(0,d,0), using the closed-form autocorrelations derived by Hosking (1981), the autocorrelation generating function can be written as:

Φν=F⁡(d,1,1−d,ν),\Phi_{\nu}=F(d,1,1-d;\nu), (6.20)

where FF is the hypergeometric function of equation (6.18), and the identity follows term by term from the Gauss series, because the series coefficients equal the autocorrelations in equation (6.16). At κ=0\kappa=0, the gross and net Sharpe ratios of the single filter and of the long-short filter are therefore closed-form under the pure fractional process, because Corollaries 5.5 and 5.4 depend on the process only through Φν\Phi_{\nu} evaluated at the filter spans.

6.4 Verification Tests

Table 6.1 verifies the closed-form Sharpe ratios within the full pipeline at the configuration of the empirical section: the long-short filter LS(250,20) under the long-memory calibration d=0.1d=0.1, which makes the cost and tail effects resolvable at the reported MC precision. The Gaussian sub-panels pair the analytic values at κ=0\kappa=0 with Gaussian simulations. The Student-t sub-panels pair the analytic values at κ=3\kappa=3 with simulations under standardized Student-t innovations with six degrees of freedom, which keep the unit variance and add an excess kurtosis of 33, close to the empirical median of 3.83.8 across our futures universe. The MC net values charge the cost against the realized turnover of equation (4.15), and the analytic net values apply the signal-turnover proxy of Proposition 4.7. The ARFIMA drift rows label the raw drift parameter μa​n=0.50\mu_{an}=0.50 of equation (6.17), and the variance scale maps it to the normalized annual drift μa​nz=μa​n/Vϕ,d\mu^{z}_{an}=\mu_{an}/\sqrt{V_{\phi,d}}: V0,0.1=Γ⁡(0.8)/Γ​(0.9)2≈1.019V_{0,0.1}=\Gamma(0.8)/\Gamma(0.9)^{2}\approx 1.019 gives 0.4950.495, and V−0.05,0.1≈1.011V_{-0.05,0.1}\approx 1.011 gives 0.4970.497. The white-noise rows carry the same convention, with μa​nz=μa​n\mu^{z}_{an}=\mu_{an} under unit variance. The analytic and the MC values both reflect the normalized drift. Both the MC and the analytic net ratios divide the cost-adjusted mean by the gross annualized volatility, matching the definition in equation (5.2). The AR-1 rows are near zero for both signs of ϕ\phi, because the two legs of the long-short filter carry the identical loading on the first lag, which cancels in the signal: the covariance in equation (5.11) reduces to q​ϕ2​(ν1−ν2)/((1−ν1​ϕ)​(1−ν2​ϕ))q\phi^{2}(\nu_{1}-\nu_{2})/\left((1-\nu_{1}\phi)(1-\nu_{2}\phi)\right), which is positive for either sign of ϕ\phi and of the second order in ϕ\phi. The single filter retains the first-order term and its Sharpe ratio changes sign with ϕ\phi, as equation (6.11) shows. Figure 6.3 verifies the formulas at the empirically calibrated d=0.02d=0.02.

The table supports three conclusions. First, the analytic values track the simulations within 0.050.05 across all processes, with the gap driven by the dampening of the autocorrelation of ztz_{t} by the lagged volatility estimator, which lowers the first-lag autocorrelation from 0.0500.050 to 0.0460.046 under the AR-1 calibration and attenuates the Sharpe ratio by 2%2\% to 8%8\% in relative terms. Second, the heavy tails lower the pooled gross Sharpe ratio by at most 0.0090.009, so the kurtosis effect is second order within the pipeline. Third, the cost of 2020bp lowers the Sharpe ratio by at most 0.020.02, while the simulated turnover exceeds the proxy by about a factor of two at the volatility span of 3333 days, as Section 4 discusses. The formulas with population moments therefore predict the realized performance of the empirical section’s filter, gross and net, under realistic tails.

7 Implementation of TF Systems

We apply the three TF systems to the universe of 8484 futures contracts in Table 7.1, which covers the most liquid contracts across global equity, bond, short-rate, currency, and commodity markets, with the volume-based trading costs of Table 7.2, which follow Exhibit B1 in Hurst et al (2017) and split by period and asset class. These costs cover rebalancing and rolling, and in our experience they are representative for a trend-following system at a medium to slow trading frequency. The proportional cost model excludes market impact, which scales nonlinearly with trade size and becomes binding for large programs.

7.1 Grid Backtests

We start with grid backtests of the TF systems, to analyze the parameter sensitivity and to select the model parameters, simulating the performance from 1 January 1997 to 10 July 2026. Each system is applied to all available futures contracts with individual profit-and-loss aggregated on the portfolio level, without portfolio risk limits. We estimate EWMA volatility using equation (2.13) for European and TSMOM TF systems with a span of 3333 days, and the ATR using equation (A.2) for American TF with the period of 3333 days. We assume that futures contracts trade in fractions, with an initial trade level of 11 USD and net profits reinvested. We consider three characteristics. The Sharpe ratio applies the arithmetic daily-moment convention of equation (5.1) to the total excess performance without management or performance fees, and returns on futures contracts are excess returns, so the Sharpe ratio requires no adjustment by the risk-free rate. The Bear Sharpe ratio conditions the excess performance on the bear regime. The annualized average costs are realized by portfolio rebalancing and computed with the volume costs in Table 7.2, and the costs reflect the turnover of each configuration. We define the bear regime as the 16%16\% of worst quarters of the long-only benchmark portfolio, because the 16%16\% tail corresponds to the one-sigma quantile of the normal distribution. For the long-only benchmark, we use the 60/40 equity/bond portfolio computed using S&P 500 index futures and the 10-year UST futures, respectively, with quarterly rebalancing. The grid contains 6464 configurations for each system. We read the grid as a sensitivity analysis rather than a strategy selection, because the maximum Sharpe ratio over a grid overstates the out-of-sample value (Sullivan et al, 1999).

For the European TF system, the two key parameters include long and short spans in days for the long-short EWMA filter in equation (2.9), where we set ν1=1−2/(long+1)\nu_{1}=1-2/(\mathrm{long}+1) and ν2=1−2/(short+1)\nu_{2}=1-2/(\mathrm{short}+1). The top row of Figure 7.1 shows the corresponding grid backtest. Fast TF with a small long span leads to high turnover and realized costs. We fix the long and short spans to 250 and 20, which provide reasonable long-term performance at moderate turnover, with realized costs of 1.7%1.7\%, in line with a typical real-world CTA system.

For the American TF system in Definition A.3, the core parameters are the spans of the long and short filters in equation (A.5) with ν1=1−2/(long+1)\nu_{1}=1-2/(\mathrm{long}+1) and ν2=1−2/(short+1)\nu_{2}=1-2/(\mathrm{short}+1). We set the entry-point scale parameter ω=5\omega=5 in equations (A.6) and (A.8) and set the stop-loss width parameter p=5p=5 in equations (A.7) and (A.9). The middle row of Figure 7.1 shows a pattern similar to the European system, with the best total and Bear Sharpe ratios around the long and short values of 250250 and 2020.

For the generalized TSMOM system in equation (A.16), the two key parameters are the period length LL in days and the number of periods MM for computing the aggregate signal. The bottom row of Figure 7.1 shows the optimal values around M=L=10M=L=10.

7.2 Comparison with SG Trend Index

We compare our three implementations of TF systems with the SG Trend Index, which tracks the performance of the 10 largest CTAs with annual rebalancing. To make a fair comparison, we apply 2%/20%2\%/20\% management/performance annual fees to performances of our TF systems. We report the excess performance of the TF systems after transaction costs and fees. The index tracks funded programs and includes their interest income, which we cannot strip out, while we keep the TF systems and the 60/40 benchmark on excess returns, so the comparison modestly favors the index.

In Figure 7.2, we show the performance of the three simulated TF systems using specifications and established optimal parameters as in Section 7.1. For European and American TF systems, we set the spans of long and short EWMA filters to 250250 and 2020, respectively. We set the static volatility target and position risk so that all three systems generate the same level of volatility of their returns. For the TSMOM system, we set the period length to L=10L=10 days and the number of periods to M=10M=10. Panels (A1), (A2i), and (B1) show that, for this choice of TF system parameters, all three systems generate similar performance in the sample period from 31 December 1999 to 10 July 2026.

From panel (C1), the three systems correlate with the SG Trend Index at 80%80\% on average, and the European and American systems correlate at 95%95\%, which indicates the robustness of different implementations with similar lookbacks. From panels (B2) and (C2), the American TF system generates about 50%50\% lower turnover and rolling costs than the European and TSMOM systems. The core distinction is that the American TF system generates discrete trades, whereas the European and TSMOM systems generate continuous signals that require more frequent rebalancing. For practical implementation of TF systems using any methodology, it is beneficial to introduce some discretization rules.

We test the Sharpe ratio differences with the robust test of Ledoit and Wolf (2008) on monthly returns net of transaction costs and net of fees, which is the basis of Figure 7.2 and the basis on which the index reports, from 31 December 1999 to 30 June 2026. The European, American, and TSMOM systems deliver annualized Sharpe ratios of 0.470.47, 0.500.50, and 0.550.55 against 0.470.47 for the SG Trend Index. The differences carry p-values of 0.960.96, 0.820.82, and 0.620.62, so the test does not reject the equality of the Sharpe ratios for any of the systems. The failure to reject is consistent with the replication claim, although it is not evidence of equivalence.

From panel (A2ii), all three systems and the SG Trend Index generate net annual returns with small dispersion, so all three specifications capture strong market trends across regimes. TF systems are weakly correlated to the 60/40 portfolio over longer periods, so TF systems are natural diversifiers of long-only portfolios.

From panel (B2), the volatility-normalized turnover ranges between 300%300\% and 400%400\% for the European and TSMOM systems and between 125%125\% and 200%200\% for the American system. A turnover of 300%300\% corresponds to a long-short equity strategy rebalancing about 25%25\% per month, while the absolute annualized turnover is close to 2000%2000\%, dominated by the low-volatility bond and rates contracts.

7.3 Attribution of Realized Sharpe Ratios to Autocorrelation and Drift

Corollary 5.5 expresses the Sharpe ratio of the European TF system through two inputs: the autocorrelation function and the drift of the volatility-normalized returns. We estimate both inputs from the futures data and test the formula against the realized backtests of all three TF systems. For each of the 84 futures contracts, we compute the volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t} with the EWMA span of 33 days, skip the first 250 days, and require at least six years of history. The signal filters initialize at zero at inception. The missing fraction of the expected response to a constant mean is νt\nu^{t}, while the standard-deviation scale under independent zero-mean input is 1−ν2​t\sqrt{1-\nu^{2t}}. At the 520-day span on the first included day, the missing mean response is 38%38\% and the standard-deviation attenuation is 8%8\%, declining to 5.6%5.6\% and below 0.2%0.2\% within two further years and averaging out over the six-year-minimum samples. The liquidity and history screens may tilt the estimates toward heavily traded markets. We estimate the sample autocorrelation function of ztz_{t} to 780 lags and the sample mean of ztz_{t}, both over the full instrument sample.

The prediction applies equation (5.12) with the sample autocorrelation function, the sample variance γ^T​(0)\hat{\gamma}_{T}(0), the variance-normalized annualized drift μ^a​nz=a​z¯T/γ^T​(0)\hat{\mu}^{z}_{an}=\sqrt{a}\,\overline{z}_{T}/\sqrt{\hat{\gamma}_{T}(0)}, and the kurtosis loading κ=0\kappa=0, which Section 6.4 justifies as a second-order effect. At the 520-day span, the truncation weight is ν780≈0.05\nu^{780}\approx 0.05, so the truncation may omit a small residual long-memory contribution at the slowest span. The validation is nonparametric, so no parametric return model is estimated. We compute two predictions for each filter span: the autocorrelation channel alone, with the drift set to zero, and the total, which adds the sample drift. Treating the population variance as known, the squared sample drift carries an upward bias of a​Var⁡[z¯T]/ϑa\,\Var[\overline{z}_{T}]/\vartheta, which equals a/T≈0.17a/T\approx 0.17 in the squared annualized drift at the six-year minimum sample under independent unit-variance returns. With the sample variance in the denominator, the expression is a first-order approximation, because the variance estimate carries its own error, and serial dependence replaces the variance of the sample mean by its long-run counterpart. The sample drift square is therefore a valid component of the in-sample decomposition and not an unbiased estimate of the population drift channel, and a forward-looking application should debias or shrink it. We compare the predictions with the Sharpe ratios of the gross backtests on the same sample, which isolates the accuracy of the formula from the accuracy of the turnover approximation. The comparison is in-sample by design: we test whether the closed form reproduces the realized performance on the same sample, including the pipeline effects that the population formulas do not capture. The out-of-sample application is a subject for future research.

Figure 7.3 pools the total predictions against the realized Sharpe ratios across instruments and spans. For the European system in panel (A), the pooled correlation is 0.990.99 and the regression slope is 0.960.96, so the formula reproduces the realized Sharpe ratio at the instrument level. Panels (B) and (C) apply the same European predictions to the realized Sharpe ratios of the American and TSMOM systems at matched lookbacks. We set the American short span to two days and the TSMOM period length to one day with the number of periods equal to the span, which a parameter search on the same sample identifies as the closest discretized counterparts of the European filter, with details in the companion repository, so the cross-system comparison is an in-sample calibrated exercise rather than an independent validation.

The TSMOM system tracks the predictions with a correlation of 0.890.89 and a slope of 0.730.73 across all spans. At the leading order, the Gaussian sign-moment identity gives a benchmark slope of 2/π≈0.80\sqrt{2/\pi}\approx 0.80 for the sign filter, so the measured TSMOM slope of 0.730.73 sits close to the Gaussian benchmark99 9 For a jointly Gaussian pair with a zero-mean unit-variance signal, 𝔼⁡[sign⁡(S)​z]=𝔼⁡[S​z]​𝔼​[|S|]=2/π​𝔼​[S​z]\mathbb{E}\left[\sgn\left(S\right)z\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[Sz\right]\mathbb{E}\left[\left|S\right|\right]=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,\mathbb{E}\left[Sz\right], which holds exactly and is the Bussgang theorem for the hard limiter. The sign transform scales the autocorrelation channel by 2/π\sqrt{2/\pi} and leaves the variance at one to the leading order, because sign2⁡(S)=1\sgn^{2}\left(S\right)=1, so the leading order refers to the Sharpe ratio mapping rather than to the moment identity..

The American system tracks the predictions with a correlation of 0.920.92 and a slope of 0.610.61 at the spans above one month, while the trailing stops and the entry buffers disengage the system from the signal at faster spans. The slopes below one measure a combined implementation discount, which mixes the nonlinear signal transformation, the lookback mapping, the entry buffers and stops, and the different risk denominators.

Figure 7.4 shows the cross-sectional medians by span with the decomposition of the prediction. The autocorrelation channel produces median Sharpe ratios from 0.550.55 at the 5-day span to 0.330.33 at the two-year span. The drift channel adds up to 0.080.08, and the contribution grows with the span as equation (6.4) predicts. The realized European medians run from 0.480.48 to 0.390.39 and sit 4%4\% to 14%14\% below the total prediction, with the largest gaps at short spans, where the error of the volatility estimator has the largest effect on fast signals, consistent with the attenuation of Section 6.4. The realized TSMOM medians run parallel to the prediction across all spans at the discount of the sign filter. The realized American medians converge to the prediction as the span grows. Thus both the TSMOM and the American TF systems can be viewed as a slow-span implementation of the same alpha.

The attribution supports the central claim of the paper with market data. Trend-following performance on liquid futures is primarily an autocorrelation phenomenon, and, in the realized in-sample decomposition, the drift channel contributes a secondary share that grows with the span. The same closed form ranks the performance across all three system designs, so the American and TSMOM systems monetize a closely related signal, and the closed form transfers to these nonlinear designs empirically rather than mathematically. The in-sample correlation validates the moment reconstruction and the limited size of the boundary, initialization, and pipeline effects, while the out-of-sample forecasting value of the estimated inputs remains to be tested. The EWMA lag-1 autocorrelation of ztz_{t} across the universe declines from about 0.040.04 in the 1990s to about 0.010.01 after 2010, with the estimation reproducible from the companion repository. Because the autocorrelation input varies slowly across decades, the estimated autocorrelation function is a candidate input for conditional span selection, and we recommend estimating the inputs on rolling windows with a debiased drift, because the formula applies conditionally on the prevailing autocorrelation function.

7.4 Skewness of Aggregated Returns

The product structure of the daily return generates positive skewness under time aggregation. The daily return multiplies the lagged signal by the current return, so the TT-day cumulative return loads on the realized autocovariance of the volatility-normalized returns at the filter lags. This loading makes the aggregated return a convex payoff on the realized trend, in line with the convexity of TF portfolios documented by Dao et al (2017), and Potters and Bouchaud (2006) document the resulting positive skewness of the exponential-average system on a random walk. Appendix D derives the third moment of the aggregated return in closed form under white noise from a single pairing identity. Proposition D.2 gives the skewness of the TT-day return of the single-filter system in equation (D.2): the skewness is zero at T=1T=1, positive at every horizon T≥2T\geq 2 although the expected return is zero, hump-shaped with the maximum near half the filter span, and independent of the loading and of the volatility target.

Panels (A) and (B) of Figure 7.5 verify and extend the closed form by simulation. Panel (A) confirms equation (D.2) at every span and horizon. Panel (B) places the three processes of Section 6 against the white-noise closed form: the AR-1 estimates track the closed form at every horizon, long memory raises the skewness at horizons short relative to the span, and at long horizons the estimates of all three processes converge to the closed form. The skewness of aggregated TF returns is therefore structural: the filter design drives the profile more than the data-generating process.

The approach is analytic beyond white noise. Under the AR-1 process, every covariance in the pairing expansion of the third moment is geometric, so the aggregated skewness admits a closed form, and the expansion generalizes to the ARFIMA process. We leave these derivations, together with the asymptotics of the horizon profile, to a follow-up paper.

The closed form is also robust to the distribution of the innovations. For independent innovations with zero mean, unit variance, and zero third moment, every surviving pairing in the third moment uses only second moments, so equation (D.2) holds without Gaussianity and without a finite-kurtosis condition. A non-zero third moment γ3\gamma_{3} of the innovations adds the single term T​γ32​∑j≥1wj3T\gamma^{2}_{3}\sum_{j\geq 1}w^{3}_{j} to the third moment of the aggregated return, with the filter weights wjw_{j} of Appendix D, and this term decays in the skewness as T−1/2T^{-1/2}. This robustness supports the application of the formula to the heavy-tailed futures returns of panel (C).

Panel (C) takes the profile to the data. For each of the 8484 contracts, we compute the gross daily returns of the single-filter European system with the span of 100100 days and zero costs, aggregate them into overlapping TT-day sums, and estimate the standardized sample skewness at each horizon. Costs shift the mean of the aggregated return and leave the skewness almost unchanged, because the skewness is invariant to the mean and the cost term is small relative to the daily return: in simulation, a cost rate of 100100bp per unit of volatility-normalized turnover changes the white-noise skewness by less than 0.0020.002 at every horizon. The cross-sectional median tracks the closed form across the full horizon range and attains 2.332.33 at the horizon of 5555 days against the closed-form value of 2.352.35, with the peak of the closed form near 5555 days. The interquartile range lies above zero at every horizon, so positive aggregated skewness is a property of the cross-section rather than of the median contract. The median sits above the closed form at short horizons, where the heavy tails and the autocorrelations of the data enter, and converges to the closed form at long horizons, in line with panel (B). Non-overlapping TT-day blocks show the same pattern, with the medians within 0.060.06 of the overlapping estimates at every horizon with sufficient data.

The proposition and the panels turn a documented property into a structural one. The positive skewness requires no autocorrelation, no drift, and no alpha, because it holds exactly under white noise where the expected return of the system is zero. The horizon profile explains why daily TF returns appear symmetric while monthly and quarterly returns are right-skewed, and it places the strongest asymmetry at horizons near half the filter span. The positive quarterly skewness of the three systems in Figure 7.2, against the negative skewness of the balanced benchmark, is consistent with this profile. The quarterly skewness of the systems in panel (A2i) of Figure 7.2 sits below the single-contract profile for two reasons that the framework quantifies. The long-short filter shifts the profile toward longer horizons, with the white-noise skewness of the LS(250,20) system at 1.71.7 at the quarterly horizon against 2.32.3 for the single filter, and the post-2000 sample realizes a quarterly skewness of 0.50.5 against 1.81.8 over the full history of the same portfolio on our data. Cross-sectional aggregation itself preserves the skewness through the common trend component, while portfolio-level volatility targeting, which the systems of Figure 7.2 do not apply, would reduce it further.

8 Conclusions

We have classified trend-following systems into European, American, and Time Series Momentum designs, and we have developed a unified analytical framework around the European system, which sizes positions with an EWMA filter of volatility-normalized returns. We have derived an exact sample-path identity for the cumulative return and closed-form gross and leading-order net Sharpe ratios under a generic stationary autocorrelation function within the linear-process class.

The closed forms separate the sources of performance. Under white noise with drift, the net Sharpe ratio under the signal-turnover proxy converges to the absolute Sharpe ratio of the instrument at long spans for any proportional cost. Under the AR-1 process, the gross Sharpe ratio is approximately 2​ϕ​a/span2\phi\sqrt{a/\mathrm{span}}, the break-even cost has the span-invariant limit c∞∗=π/(2​a)​ϕ/(1−ϕ)c^{*}_{\infty}=\sqrt{\pi/(2a)}\,\phi/(1-\phi), and costs determine the viability of a short-memory alpha to first order. Under the ARFIMA process with memory parameter dd, the net Sharpe ratio attains an interior cost-optimal span, which scales as c1/(2​d)c^{1/(2d)} in the large-cost limit with the net-to-gross ratio converging to 4​d/(1+2​d)4d/(1+2d).

We have verified the framework by simulation and on market data. Within the full pipeline, the formulas track the simulated gross and net Sharpe ratios within 0.050.05. On 84 liquid futures contracts, the sample autocorrelation function and drift reproduce the realized Sharpe ratios of the European system with a pooled correlation of 0.990.99 and a slope of 0.960.96, and they rank the TSMOM and American systems at design-specific implementation discounts. Trend-following performance is primarily an autocorrelation phenomenon with a drift share that grows with the span. At realized costs of 4040bp to 6060bp per unit of turnover, the proxy break-even cost implied by the observed short-lag autocorrelation lies below the realized cost level, while the long-memory component supports positive net performance at the one-to-three-month spans. We prove that under white noise the skewness of the aggregated return admits the closed form of Proposition D.2, positive at every horizon beyond one day and peaking near half the filter span. We show that under general empirical and theoretical data generation processes that the TF skewness is positive, so the defensive right tail of TF returns is structural.

The framework connects trend-following to the theory of stationary processes: a TF system is a spectral instrument, whose filter span selects the bandwidth of a Poisson kernel and whose alpha is the excess spectral mass of the volatility-normalized returns at low frequencies. The cost-optimal span solves a bandwidth-selection problem against the spectral shape and the cost level, with the AR-1 and ARFIMA asymptotics as its two tractable instances. The sign-based designs point to an extension to nonlinear filters, and we develop the diversification benefits of TF portfolios for long-only investors in a companion paper.

Appendix A American and TSMOM TF Systems

The American TF system applies the average true range (ATR) of daily prices for the signal buffer, the position size, and the stop-loss levels.

Definition A.1 (Average True Range (ATR)).

The daily true range is computed by:

t​rt=max⁡{|h​lt|,|h​ct|,|l​ct|},h​lt=sh​i​g​ht−sl​o​wt,hct=sh​i​g​ht−sc​l​o​s​et−1,lct=sl​o​wt−sc​l​o​s​et−1,\begin{split}tr_{t}&=\max\left\{\left|hl_{t}\right|,\left|hc_{t}\right|,\left|lc_{t}\right|\right\},\\ hl_{t}&=s^{high}_{t}-s^{low}_{t},\ hc_{t}=s^{high}_{t}-s^{close}_{t-1},\ lc_{t}=s^{low}_{t}-s^{close}_{t-1},\end{split} (A.1)

where sth​i​g​h,stl​o​w,stc​l​o​s​es^{high}_{t},s^{low}_{t},s^{close}_{t} are daily high, low, and close prices at the tt-th day.

ATR over a period of NN days is computed as the average of daily true ranges by:

A​T​Rt=1N​∑n=0N−1t​rt−n.ATR_{t}=\frac{1}{N}\sum^{N-1}_{n=0}tr_{t-n}. (A.2)

ATR is a dimensional, price-measured variable, similar to the price volatility in equation (2.12). To construct an ATR-based estimator analogous to the EWMA returns-volatility estimator in equation (2.13), we introduce the relative true range and its EWMA filter.

Definition A.2 (Relative True Range (RTR)).

Daily RTR is computed by:

r​t​rt=t​rtst−1c​l​o​s​e.rtr_{t}=\frac{tr_{t}}{s^{close}_{t-1}}. (A.3)

EWMA of RTR is denoted by ERTR and computed using EWMA filter:

E​R​T​Rt=ℒ(νe​t​r)​(t​rtst−1c​l​o​s​e),ERTR_{t}=\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{etr})}\left(\frac{tr_{t}}{s^{close}_{t-1}}\right), (A.4)

where νe​t​r\nu_{etr} is the smoothing parameter. The ERTR provides the volatility input of the American TF system, as the EWMA volatility of equation (2.13) serves the European system.

A.1 American TF System

For the American TF system, we work with the sequence of daily prices {st}\{s_{t}\} as follows.

Definition A.3 (American TF System).
  • •

    s¯(ν1)=ℒ(ν1)​(st),s¯(ν2)=ℒ(ν2)​(st),\overline{s}^{(\nu_{1})}=\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{1})}(s_{t}),\ \overline{s}^{(\nu_{2})}=\mathcal{L}^{(\nu_{2})}(s_{t}), (A.5)

    where ν1>ν2\nu_{1}>\nu_{2}.

  • •

    If the current position is zero, the long position is initiated when the fast filter exceeds the slow filter plus the signal buffer as follows:

    s¯(ν2)>s¯(ν1)+ω⋅A​T​Rt,\overline{s}^{(\nu_{2})}>\overline{s}^{(\nu_{1})}+\omega\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.6)

    where ω\omega is the entry-point width parameter. The position size pl​o​n​gp^{long} and the stop loss s​ltl​o​n​gsl^{long}_{t} are initiated respectively by:

    pl​o​n​g=R​stA​T​Rt,s​ltl​o​n​g=st−p⋅A​T​Rt,p^{long}=R\frac{s_{t}}{ATR_{t}},\ sl^{long}_{t}=s_{t}-p\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.7)

    where RR is the risk multiple and pp is the stop-loss width parameter.

    The short position is initiated when the fast filter drops below the slow filter minus the buffer:

    s¯(ν2)<s¯(ν1)−ω⋅A​T​Rt,\overline{s}^{(\nu_{2})}<\overline{s}^{(\nu_{1})}-\omega\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.8)

    where the entry-point scale ω\omega matches the long side in equation (A.6) for robustness. The position size ps​h​o​r​tp^{short} and the stop loss are initiated by:

    ps​h​o​r​t=−R​stA​T​Rt,s​lts​h​o​r​t=st+p⋅A​T​Rt,p^{short}=-R\frac{s_{t}}{ATR_{t}},\ sl^{short}_{t}=s_{t}+p\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.9)

    with the risk multiple RR and the stop-loss width pp of equation (A.7).

    If the current position is non-zero, the long position is closed when the stop-loss is breached and the signal in equation (A.6) is off1010 10 A stop breach while the signal of equation (A.6) remains on would re-create the position on the next trading day, so the exit requires both the stop breach and the signal turning off.:

    st<s​lt−1l​o​n​g&s¯(ν2)≤s¯(ν1)+ω⋅A​T​Rt,s_{t}<sl^{long}_{t-1}\ \&\ \overline{s}^{(\nu_{2})}\leq\overline{s}^{(\nu_{1})}+\omega\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.10)

    otherwise the stop-loss is updated as follows:

    s​ltl​o​n​g=max⁡{s​lt−1l​o​n​g,st−p⋅A​T​Rt}.sl^{long}_{t}=\max\left\{sl^{long}_{t-1},s_{t}-p\cdot ATR_{t}\right\}. (A.11)

    The short position is closed if the stop-loss is breached and the condition in equation (A.8) is off:

    st>s​lt−1s​h​o​r​t&s¯(ν2)≥s¯(ν1)−ω⋅A​T​Rt,s_{t}>sl^{short}_{t-1}\ \&\ \overline{s}^{(\nu_{2})}\geq\overline{s}^{(\nu_{1})}-\omega\cdot ATR_{t}, (A.12)

    otherwise the stop-loss is updated by the analogous minimum:

    s​lts​h​o​r​t=min⁡{s​lt−1s​h​o​r​t,st+p⋅A​T​Rt}.sl^{short}_{t}=\min\left\{sl^{short}_{t-1},s_{t}+p\cdot ATR_{t}\right\}. (A.13)

The risk multiple RR sets the notional risk budget per trade: the initial stop distance p⋅A​T​Rt/stp\cdot ATR_{t}/s_{t} times the weight pl​o​n​gp^{long} equals R​pR\,p of the notional.

The American system differs from the European system in two ways. The position size is fixed at trade inception using the current ATR, and the exit is a trailing stop-loss rather than a signal reversal, so a continuing trend raises the stop and defers the exit. The position quantity pl​o​n​gp^{long} in equation (A.7) is a dimensionless notional weight, so we state the per-trade P&L per unit of notional capital. The long position exits at the first day τl​o​n​g\tau^{long} on which both conditions of equation (A.10) hold, and the short position at the first day τs​h​o​r​t\tau^{short} on which both conditions of equation (A.12) hold, so the P&L of the trade is exact:

P&Ll​o​n​g=pl​o​n​g​(sτl​o​n​gs0−1),P&Ls​h​o​r​t=ps​h​o​r​t​(sτs​h​o​r​ts0−1),\text{P\&L}^{long}=p^{long}\left(\frac{s_{\tau^{long}}}{s_{0}}-1\right),\qquad\text{P\&L}^{short}=p^{short}\left(\frac{s_{\tau^{short}}}{s_{0}}-1\right), (A.14)

where s0s_{0} is the entry price at the day t0t_{0}. The recursion in equation (A.11) unwinds over the life of the trade to s​ltl​o​n​g=maxt0≤u≤t⁡{su−p⋅A​T​Ru}sl^{long}_{t}=\max_{t_{0}\leq u\leq t}\left\{s_{u}-p\cdot ATR_{u}\right\}, so the exit price is close to sm​a​x−p⋅A​T​Rs_{max}-p\cdot ATR for the long position and to sm​i​n+p⋅A​T​Rs_{min}+p\cdot ATR for the short position, with the maximum price sm​a​xs_{max} and the minimum price sm​i​ns_{min} over the life of the trade. Both expressions are heuristics, and they require three conditions: the entry signal is off already at the first breach of the stop, by equation (A.6) for the long position and by equation (A.8) for the short position, the ATR is approximately constant over the life of the trade, and the price gaps and the execution slippage are ignored. The backtest applies the notional weights and accrues the P&L through the weighted returns, with the filters, the stops, and the ATR of the day tt determining the position that earns the return of the day t+1t+1.

A.2 Time Series Momentum (TSMOM) System

Moskowitz et al (2012), Hurst et al (2013), and Baltas (2015) construct the TSMOM signal as the average sign of rolling 12 monthly returns:

wt=1M​∑m=1Msign⁡(st−m+1st−m−11−1)​σtargetσt−1a​n,w_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum^{M}_{m=1}\sgn\left(\frac{s_{t-m+1}}{s_{t-m-11}}-1\right)\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sigma^{an}_{t-1}}, (A.15)

where sign⁡(x)\sgn(x) is the sign function, {st}\{s_{t}\} is the set of month-end prices, σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}} is the annualized volatility target, and σta​n\sigma^{an}_{t} is the annualized volatility estimate. Dudler et al (2015) extend this approach to averaging the signs of volatility-normalized returns.

We generalize this approach as follows. We fix a period length of LL days and define the rebalancing grid {t′}\{t^{\prime}\} as the multiples of LL, t′≡0​(mod L)t^{\prime}\equiv 0\ \text{(mod L)}. We set the lookback to MM periods, so the signal aggregates M​LML daily observations. We replace the sign of the aggregated return with the sum of the signs of the period returns, which yields the exact unit-variance normalization below.

Definition A.4 (TSMOM).

The signal is the normalized sum of the signs of daily volatility-normalized returns over the lookback of MM periods with LL days each:

wt′=σtargetσt′−1a​n​St′,St′=1M​L​∑m=1Mbt′−(m−1)​L,bt′′=∑t=t′′−L+1t′′sign⁡(rtσt−1a​n),w_{t^{\prime}}=\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}}{\sigma^{an}_{t^{\prime}-1}}\,S_{t^{\prime}},\quad S_{t^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{ML}}\sum^{M}_{m=1}b_{t^{\prime}-(m-1)L},\quad b_{t^{\prime\prime}}=\sum^{t^{\prime\prime}}_{t=t^{\prime\prime}-L+1}\sgn\left(\frac{r_{t}}{\sigma^{an}_{t-1}}\right), (A.16)

where σta​n\sigma^{an}_{t} is the annualized volatility of daily returns. We extrapolate wt′w_{t^{\prime}} to the daily grid {t}\{t\} by forward fill. The weight wt′w_{t^{\prime}} uses returns through day t′t^{\prime} and applies from the return of day t′+1t^{\prime}+1 onward, so the forward fill introduces no same-day look-ahead.

In equation (A.16), the double sum contains M​LML daily signs. Under serially independent returns whose distribution is continuous at zero with zero median, the signs are independent Rademacher variables with unit variance, so the sum has variance M​LML and the normalized signal St′S_{t^{\prime}} is a zz-score. An atom at zero would lower the variance of the sign. The annualized volatility of the system return for each instrument is therefore approximately σtarget\sigma_{\mathrm{target}} independently of MM and LL, and the sign function removes the volatility estimator from the signal because sign⁡(rt/σt−1a​n)=sign⁡(rt)\sgn(r_{t}/\sigma^{an}_{t-1})=\sgn(r_{t}). The double sum reindexes to a single sum of M​LML daily signs over disjoint blocks, so the signal value depends on the meta parameters (L,M)(L,M) only through the product M​LML, while LL sets the rebalancing frequency.

Appendix C Asymptotics of the Cost-Optimal Span

This appendix formalizes the asymptotic statements of Section 6 on the cost-optimal span. Throughout, we consider the zero-drift case with κ=0\kappa=0 and the single variance-preserving filter, we write η=1−ν=2/(span+1)\eta=1-\nu=2/(\mathrm{span}+1), we set c0=2​a​c/πc_{0}=2ac/\sqrt{\pi}, and S​Rn​e​tSR^{net} denotes the leading-order form of equation (5.13), which charges the cost against the signal-turnover proxy of Proposition 4.6. The break-even and optimal-span results therefore describe the independence-based proxy cost model, and Section 6.4 quantifies the pipeline turnover in excess of it. The gross Sharpe ratio and the cost drag share the factor 1/Bν+Aν21/\sqrt{B_{\nu}+A^{2}_{\nu}}, so the net Sharpe ratio in equation (5.13) takes the form:

S​Rn​e​t​(η)=η​M​(η)W⁡(η),M⁡(η)=a​Aνη−c02−η,W⁡(η)=Bν+Aν2η.SR^{net}(\eta)=\frac{\sqrt{\eta}\,M(\eta)}{\sqrt{W(\eta)}},\qquad M(\eta)=\frac{\sqrt{a}\,A_{\nu}}{\eta}-\frac{c_{0}}{\sqrt{2-\eta}},\qquad W(\eta)=\frac{B_{\nu}+A^{2}_{\nu}}{\eta}. (C.1)

Remark C.3 (White noise with drift).

Under the zero-autocorrelation process with drift μa​nz≠0\mu^{z}_{an}\neq 0, direct differentiation of equation (6.4) shows that the gross Sharpe ratio increases in the span with the limit |μa​nz||\mu^{z}_{an}|, while the proxy cost drag declines to zero. The net Sharpe ratio under the signal-turnover proxy therefore converges to |μa​nz||\mu^{z}_{an}| for every proportional cost, which formalizes the buy-and-hold limit of Section 6, up to a deterministic scale. The limit describes the proxy cost model: the mean of the variance-preserving signal grows as μa​nz​span\mu^{z}_{an}\sqrt{\mathrm{span}}, so, with an estimated volatility, the omitted volatility-update turnover need not vanish at long spans.

Appendix D Skewness of Aggregated Returns under White Noise

Let the volatility-normalized returns ztz_{t} be independent standard normal. Write the unit-variance signal as St−1=∑j≥1wj​zt−jS_{t-1}=\sum_{j\geq 1}w_{j}z_{t-j} with ∑j≥1wj2=1\sum_{j\geq 1}w^{2}_{j}=1 and the signal autocorrelation R⁡(h)=∑j≥1wj​wj+hR(h)=\sum_{j\geq 1}w_{j}w_{j+h}. The daily system return is ft=St−1​ztf_{t}=S_{t-1}z_{t} up to the loading and the volatility target, which scale ftf_{t} linearly and cancel in the skewness. For the single filter, wj=1−ν2​νj−1w_{j}=\sqrt{1-\nu^{2}}\,\nu^{j-1} and R⁡(h)=νhR(h)=\nu^{h}.

Lemma D.1 (Pairing identity for third-order moments).

For h≥1h\geq 1, 𝔼⁡[ft2​ft−h]=2​wh​R​(h)\mathbb{E}\left[f^{2}_{t}f_{t-h}\right]=2w_{h}R(h). All other third-order moments vanish: 𝔼⁡[ft3]=0\mathbb{E}\left[f^{3}_{t}\right]=0, 𝔼⁡[ft2​ft+h]=0\mathbb{E}\left[f^{2}_{t}f_{t+h}\right]=0, and 𝔼⁡[ft​fs​fu]=0\mathbb{E}\left[f_{t}f_{s}f_{u}\right]=0 for distinct tt, ss, uu.

Proof.

The return ztz_{t} is independent of all signals and returns up to time tt. In 𝔼⁡[ft3]=𝔼⁡[St−13]​𝔼​[zt3]\mathbb{E}\left[f^{3}_{t}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[S^{3}_{t-1}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[z^{3}_{t}\right], both factors vanish for centred Gaussians. In 𝔼⁡[ft2​ft+h]\mathbb{E}\left[f^{2}_{t}f_{t+h}\right] and in 𝔼⁡[ft​fs​fu]\mathbb{E}\left[f_{t}f_{s}f_{u}\right] with t>s>ut>s>u, the return with the largest time index enters the product exactly once, so the expectation vanishes under the Isserlis theorem. For the surviving moment, the independence of ztz_{t} gives 𝔼⁡[ft2​ft−h]=𝔼⁡[St−12​St−h−1​zt−h]\mathbb{E}\left[f^{2}_{t}f_{t-h}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[S^{2}_{t-1}S_{t-h-1}z_{t-h}\right]. We decompose St−1=wh​zt−h+RhS_{t-1}=w_{h}z_{t-h}+R_{h}, where RhR_{h} collects the remaining innovations and is independent of zt−hz_{t-h}. Expanding the square, the terms with an odd total power of zt−hz_{t-h} vanish, and the cross term gives 2​wh​𝔼​[zt−h2]​𝔼​[Rh​St−h−1]=2​wh​R​(h)2w_{h}\,\mathbb{E}\left[z^{2}_{t-h}\right]\mathbb{E}\left[R_{h}S_{t-h-1}\right]=2w_{h}R(h), because St−h−1S_{t-h-1} contains no zt−hz_{t-h}, so that 𝔼⁡[Rh​St−h−1]=𝔼⁡[St−1​St−h−1]=R⁡(h)\mathbb{E}\left[R_{h}S_{t-h-1}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[S_{t-1}S_{t-h-1}\right]=R(h). ∎

Lemma D.1 annihilates all but the paired terms with the later index squared, so 𝔼⁡[FT3]=3​∑t>s𝔼⁡[ft2​fs]=6​∑h=1T−1(T−h)​wh​R​(h)\mathbb{E}\left[F^{3}_{T}\right]=3\sum_{t>s}\mathbb{E}\left[f^{2}_{t}f_{s}\right]=6\sum^{T-1}_{h=1}\left(T-h\right)w_{h}R(h). For the single filter, wh​R​(h)=1−ν2​ν2​h−1w_{h}R(h)=\sqrt{1-\nu^{2}}\,\nu^{2h-1}, and the identity ∑h=1T−1(T−h)​xh=x⁡(T⁡(1−x)−1+xT)/(1−x)2\sum^{T-1}_{h=1}\left(T-h\right)x^{h}=x\left(T\left(1-x\right)-1+x^{T}\right)/\left(1-x\right)^{2} with x=ν2x=\nu^{2} yields equation (D.2). For positivity, the function g⁡(x)=T⁡(1−x)−1+xTg(x)=T\left(1-x\right)-1+x^{T} satisfies g⁡(1)=0g(1)=0 and g′​(x)=−T⁡(1−xT−1)<0g^{\prime}(x)=-T\left(1-x^{T-1}\right)<0 on (0,1)\left(0,1\right), so g⁡(ν2)>0g\left(\nu^{2}\right)>0 for T≥2T\geq 2, while gg vanishes identically at T=1T=1. ∎

The long-short filter satisfies Lemma D.1 with its own weights and autocorrelation, so its third moment follows from equation (D.1) with the long-short whw_{h} and R⁡(h)R(h). Under a general stationary autocorrelation function, additional pairings of the order of the autocorrelations enter the third-order moments, so the white-noise profile gives the leading-order skewness for weakly autocorrelated returns. Under the AR-1 process, the additional pairings form geometric sums, so the third moment remains closed-form, and the expansion generalizes to the ARFIMA process. We develop the general case and the asymptotics of the profile in the follow-up paper.
